cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is social psychology?
cards.back: Social psychology is that branch of psychology which investigates how the behaviour of individuals is affected by others and the social environment.
cards.quote: Social psychology is that branch of psychology which investigates how the behaviour of individuals is affected by others and the social environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In order to understand completely how the social context influences the individual, it is necessary to study both ____ and social behaviour.
cards.back: In order to understand completely how the social context influences the individual, it is necessary to study both social-cognitive processes and social behaviour.
cards.quote: In order to understand completely how the social context influences the individual, it is necessary to study both social-cognitive processes and social behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is an attitude? What do all definitions of attitude agree on?
cards.back: All definitions of attitudes agree that an attitude is a state of the mind, a set of views, or thoughts, regarding some topic (called the ‘attitude object’), which have an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral quality).
cards.quote: All definitions of attitudes agree that an attitude is a state of the mind, a set of views, or thoughts, regarding some topic (called the ‘attitude object’), which have an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral quality).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three aspects (components) of an attitude.
cards.back:
cognitive aspect
affective aspect
behavioural (or conative) aspect
cards.quote: The thought component is referred to as the cognitive aspect, the emotional component is known as the affective aspect, and the tendency to act is called the behavioural (or conative) aspect.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Taken together, these three aspects have been referred to as the ____ components (Affective-Behavioural-Cognitive components) of attitude.
cards.back: Taken together, these three aspects have been referred to as the A-B-C components (Affective-Behavioural-Cognitive components) of attitude.
cards.quote: Taken together, these three aspects have been referred to as the A-B-C components (Affective-Behavioural-Cognitive components) of attitude.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Note that attitudes are themselves not behaviour, but they represent a ____ to behave or act in certain ways.
cards.back: Note that attitudes are themselves not behaviour, but they represent a tendency to behave or act in certain ways.
cards.quote: Note that attitudes are themselves not behaviour, but they represent a tendency to behave or act in certain ways.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Your view of a ‘green environment’ is positive, based on sufficient information. Which A-B-C component is this?
cards.back:
Cognitive (‘C’) component, along with the evaluative aspect
Based on sufficient information about the environment, your view towards a ‘green environment’ is positive (cognitive or ‘C’ component, along with the evaluative aspect).
cards.quote: Based on sufficient information about the environment, your view towards a ‘green environment’ is positive (cognitive or ‘C’ component, along with the evaluative aspect).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: You feel happy at greenery and sad and angry when trees are cut down. Which component of the attitude?
cards.back:
Affective (emotional), or ‘A’ component
These aspects reflect the affective (emotional), or ‘A’ component of the same attitude.
cards.quote: These aspects reflect the affective (emotional), or ‘A’ component of the same attitude.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: You actively take part in a tree plantation campaign. Which component of the ‘green environment’ attitude is this?
cards.back:
Behavioural, or ‘B’ component
This shows the behavioural or ‘B’ component of your attitudes towards a ‘green environment’.
cards.quote: This shows the behavioural or ‘B’ component of your attitudes towards a ‘green environment’.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In general, we expect all three components to be ____ with each other, that is, in the same direction.
cards.back: In general, we expect all three components to be consistent with each other, that is, in the same direction.
cards.quote: In general, we expect all three components to be consistent with each other, that is, in the same direction.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are beliefs (in relation to attitudes)?
cards.back: Beliefs refer to the cognitive component of attitudes, and form the ground on which attitudes stand, such as belief in God, or belief in democracy as a political ideology.
cards.quote: Beliefs refer to the cognitive component of attitudes, and form the ground on which attitudes stand, such as belief in God, or belief in democracy as a political ideology.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are values (in relation to attitudes and beliefs)?
cards.back: Values are attitudes or beliefs that contain a ‘should’ or ‘ought’ aspect, such as moral or ethical values.
cards.quote: Values are attitudes or beliefs that contain a ‘should’ or ‘ought’ aspect, such as moral or ethical values.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What purpose is served by an attitude?
cards.back: We find that attitudes provide a background that makes it easier for a person to decide how to act in new situations.
cards.quote: We find that attitudes provide a background that makes it easier for a person to decide how to act in new situations.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the four significant features (properties) of attitudes.
cards.back:
Valence (positivity or negativity)
Extremeness
Simplicity or Complexity (multiplexity)
Centrality
cards.quote: Four significant features of attitudes are : Valence (positivity or negativity), Extremeness, Simplicity or Complexity (multiplexity), and Centrality.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the valence of an attitude?
cards.back: The valence of an attitude tells us whether an attitude is positive or negative towards the attitude object.
cards.quote: The valence of an attitude tells us whether an attitude is positive or negative towards the attitude object.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the extremeness of an attitude?
cards.back: The extremeness of an attitude indicates how positive or negative an attitude is.
cards.quote: The extremeness of an attitude indicates how positive or negative an attitude is.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is simplicity or complexity (multiplexity) of an attitude?
cards.back: Simplicity or Complexity (multiplexity) : This feature refers to how many attitudes there are within a broader attitude.
cards.quote: Simplicity or Complexity (multiplexity) : This feature refers to how many attitudes there are within a broader attitude.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is an attitude system said to be ‘simple’ and when ‘complex’?
cards.back: An attitude system is said to be ‘simple’ if it contains only one or a few attitudes, and ‘complex’ if it is made up of many attitudes.
cards.quote: An attitude system is said to be ‘simple’ if it contains only one or a few attitudes, and ‘complex’ if it is made up of many attitudes.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Each member attitude that belongs to an attitude system also has ____ components.
cards.back: Each member attitude that belongs to an attitude system also has A-B-C components.
cards.quote: Each member attitude that belongs to an attitude system also has A-B-C components.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is centrality of an attitude?
cards.back: Centrality : This refers to the role of a particular attitude in the attitude system.
cards.quote: Centrality : This refers to the role of a particular attitude in the attitude system.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: An attitude with greater ____ would influence the other attitudes in the system much more than non-central (or peripheral) attitudes would.
cards.back: An attitude with greater centrality would influence the other attitudes in the system much more than non-central (or peripheral) attitudes would.
cards.quote: An attitude with greater centrality would influence the other attitudes in the system much more than non-central (or peripheral) attitudes would.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A negative attitude towards high military expenditure within the attitude towards world peace shows which property?
cards.back:
Centrality
For example, in the attitude towards world peace, a negative attitude towards high military expenditure may be present as a core or central attitude that influences all other attitudes in the multiple attitude system.
cards.quote: For example, in the attitude towards world peace, a negative attitude towards high military expenditure may be present as a core or central attitude that influences all other attitudes in the multiple attitude system.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How are attitudes in general acquired, according to NCERT?
cards.back: In general, attitudes are learned through one’s own experiences, and through interaction with others.
cards.quote: In general, attitudes are learned through one’s own experiences, and through interaction with others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A student likes a subject because of the teacher. Which process of attitude formation is this?
cards.back:
Learning attitudes by association
In other words, a positive attitude towards the subject is learned through the positive association between a teacher and a student.
cards.quote: In other words, a positive attitude towards the subject is learned through the positive association between a teacher and a student.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A teenager who does yogasanas regularly is honoured as ‘Miss Good Health’ in school. Which process of learning is this?
cards.back:
Learning attitudes by being rewarded or punished
For example, if a teenager does yogasanas regularly, and gets the honour of being ‘Miss Good Health’ in her school, she may develop a positive attitude towards yoga and health in general.
cards.quote: For example, if a teenager does yogasanas regularly, and gets the honour of being ‘Miss Good Health’ in her school, she may develop a positive attitude towards yoga and health in general.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Children form a respectful attitude to elders by seeing their parents respect elders. Which process is this?
cards.back:
Learning attitudes through modelling (observing others)
For example, children may form a respectful attitude towards elders, by observing that their parents show respect for elders, and are appreciated for it.
cards.quote: For example, children may form a respectful attitude towards elders, by observing that their parents show respect for elders, and are appreciated for it.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are norms?
cards.back: Norms are unwritten rules about behaviour that everyone is supposed to show under specific circumstances.
cards.quote: Norms are unwritten rules about behaviour that everyone is supposed to show under specific circumstances.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Reading the biographies of self-actualised persons leads to a positive attitude to hard work. Which process?
cards.back:
Learning through exposure to information
By reading the biographies of self-actualised persons, an individual may develop a positive attitude towards hard work and other aspects as the means of achieving success in life.
cards.quote: By reading the biographies of self-actualised persons, an individual may develop a positive attitude towards hard work and other aspects as the means of achieving success in life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which agents shape attitudes in the early years of life, and which become important later?
cards.back: Particularly in the early years of life, parents and other family members play a significant role in shaping attitude formation. Later, the school environment becomes an important background for attitude formation.
cards.quote: Particularly in the early years of life, parents and other family members play a significant role in shaping attitude formation. Later, the school environment becomes an important background for attitude formation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What do reference groups indicate to an individual?
cards.back: Reference groups indicate to an individual the norms regarding acceptable behaviour and ways of thinking.
cards.quote: Reference groups indicate to an individual the norms regarding acceptable behaviour and ways of thinking.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is the influence of reference groups on attitudes especially noticeable?
cards.back: Their influence is noticeable especially during the beginning of adolescence, at which time it is important for the individual to feel that s/he belongs to a group.
cards.quote: Their influence is noticeable especially during the beginning of adolescence, at which time it is important for the individual to feel that s/he belongs to a group.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How can the media be used to influence attitudes, for good and bad?
cards.back: The media can be used to create consumerist attitudes where none existed, and can also be harnessed to create positive attitudes to facilitate social harmony.
cards.quote: The media can be used to create consumerist attitudes where none existed, and can also be harnessed to create positive attitudes to facilitate social harmony.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How are values formed?
cards.back: Values are formed when a particular belief or attitude becomes an inseparable part of the person’s outlook on life.
cards.quote: Values are formed when a particular belief or attitude becomes an inseparable part of the person’s outlook on life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How are attitudes learnt through modelling?
cards.back: Instead, we learn them by observing others being rewarded or punished for expressing thoughts, or showing behaviour of a particular kind towards the attitude object.
cards.quote: Instead, we learn them by observing others being rewarded or punished for expressing thoughts, or showing behaviour of a particular kind towards the attitude object.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Learning attitudes through group or cultural norms is an example of which forms of learning?
cards.back: Learning attitudes through group or cultural norms may actually be an example of all three forms of learning described above — learning through association, reward or punishment, and modelling.
cards.quote: Learning attitudes through group or cultural norms may actually be an example of all three forms of learning described above — learning through association, reward or punishment, and modelling.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which attitudes are more likely to change: those in the formative stage or those firmly established?
cards.back: Attitudes that are still in the formative stage, and are more like opinions, are much more likely to change compared to attitudes that have become firmly established, and have become a part of the individual’s values.
cards.quote: Attitudes that are still in the formative stage, and are more like opinions, are much more likely to change compared to attitudes that have become firmly established, and have become a part of the individual’s values.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who proposed the concept of balance, and what is it described as?
cards.back: The concept of balance, proposed by Fritz Heider is sometimes described in the form of the ‘P-O-X’ triangle, which represents the relationships between three aspects or components of the attitude.
cards.quote: The concept of balance, proposed by Fritz Heider is sometimes described in the form of the ‘P-O-X’ triangle, which represents the relationships between three aspects or components of the attitude.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Heider’s P-O-X triangle, what do P, O and X stand for?
cards.back: P is the person whose attitude is being studied, O is another person, and X is the topic towards which the attitude is being studied (attitude object).
cards.quote: P is the person whose attitude is being studied, O is another person, and X is the topic towards which the attitude is being studied (attitude object).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The basic idea is that an attitude changes if there is a state of ____ between the P-O attitude, O-X attitude, and P-X attitude.
cards.back: The basic idea is that an attitude changes if there is a state of imbalance between the P-O attitude, O-X attitude, and P-X attitude.
cards.quote: The basic idea is that an attitude changes if there is a state of imbalance between the P-O attitude, O-X attitude, and P-X attitude.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is imbalance found in the P-O-X triangle?
cards.back: Imbalance is found when (i) all three sides of the P-O-X triangle are negative, or (ii) two sides are positive, and one side is negative.
cards.quote: Imbalance is found when (i) all three sides of the P-O-X triangle are negative, or (ii) two sides are positive, and one side is negative.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is balance found in the P-O-X triangle?
cards.back: Balance is found when (i) all three sides are positive, or (ii) two sides are negative, and one side is positive.
cards.quote: Balance is found when (i) all three sides are positive, or (ii) two sides are negative, and one side is positive.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Dowry example: P-X positive, O-P positive, O-X negative. Balance or imbalance?
cards.back:
Imbalance
That is, there are two positives and one negative in the triangle. This is a situation of imbalance.
cards.quote: That is, there are two positives and one negative in the triangle. This is a situation of imbalance.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who proposed the concept of cognitive dissonance, and which component does it emphasise?
cards.back: The concept of cognitive dissonance was proposed by Leon Festinger. It emphasises the cognitive component.
cards.quote: The concept of cognitive dissonance was proposed by Leon Festinger. It emphasises the cognitive component.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: If an individual finds that two cognitions in an attitude are ____, then one of them will be changed in the direction of consonance.
cards.back: If an individual finds that two cognitions in an attitude are dissonant, then one of them will be changed in the direction of consonance.
cards.quote: If an individual finds that two cognitions in an attitude are dissonant, then one of them will be changed in the direction of consonance.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ‘Pan masala causes mouth cancer’ and ‘I eat pan masala’: what state do these two cognitions create?
cards.back:
Cognitive dissonance
Holding these two ideas or cognitions will make any individual feel that something is ‘out of tune’, or dissonant, in the attitude towards pan masala.
cards.quote: Holding these two ideas or cognitions will make any individual feel that something is ‘out of tune’, or dissonant, in the attitude towards pan masala.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which two social psychologists conducted the experiment that showed how cognitive dissonance works?
cards.back: Festinger and Carlsmith, two social psychologists, conducted an experiment that showed how cognitive dissonance works (see Box 6.2).
cards.quote: Festinger and Carlsmith, two social psychologists, conducted an experiment that showed how cognitive dissonance works (see Box 6.2).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In the Festinger-Carlsmith experiment, which group rated the boring experiment as more interesting, $ 1 or $ 20?
cards.back: The responses showed that the $ 1 group described the experiment as more interesting than the $ 20 group.
cards.quote: The responses showed that the $ 1 group described the experiment as more interesting than the $ 20 group.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does cognitive consistency mean?
cards.back: Cognitive consistency means that two components, aspects or elements of the attitude, or attitude system, must be in the same direction.
cards.quote: Cognitive consistency means that two components, aspects or elements of the attitude, or attitude system, must be in the same direction.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Both balance and cognitive dissonance are examples of ____.
cards.back: Both balance and cognitive dissonance are examples of cognitive consistency.
cards.quote: Both balance and cognitive dissonance are examples of cognitive consistency.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who proposed the two-step concept of attitude change, and what does it say?
cards.back: The two-step concept was proposed by S.M. Mohsin, an Indian psychologist. According to him, attitude change takes place in the form of two steps.
cards.quote: The two-step concept was proposed by S.M. Mohsin, an Indian psychologist. According to him, attitude change takes place in the form of two steps.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In the two-step concept, who are the ‘target’ and the ‘source’?
cards.back: The ‘target’ is the person whose attitude is to be changed. The ‘source’ is the person through whose influence the change is to take place.
cards.quote: The ‘target’ is the person whose attitude is to be changed. The ‘source’ is the person through whose influence the change is to take place.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does identification mean in the two-step concept?
cards.back: Identification means that the target has liking and regard for the source.
cards.quote: Identification means that the target has liking and regard for the source.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which are easier to change: positive attitudes or negative attitudes?
cards.back: In general, positive attitudes are easier to change than negative attitudes are.
cards.quote: In general, positive attitudes are easier to change than negative attitudes are.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which attitudes are more difficult to change: extreme and central, or less extreme and peripheral?
cards.back: Extreme attitudes, and central attitudes are more difficult to change than the less extreme, and peripheral (less significant) attitudes are.
cards.quote: Extreme attitudes, and central attitudes are more difficult to change than the less extreme, and peripheral (less significant) attitudes are.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which are easier to change: simple attitudes or multiple attitudes?
cards.back: Simple attitudes are easier to change than multiple attitudes are.
cards.quote: Simple attitudes are easier to change than multiple attitudes are.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is a congruent attitude change?
cards.back: An attitude change may be congruent — it may change in the same direction as the existing attitude (for example, a positive attitude may become more positive, or a negative attitude may become more negative).
cards.quote: An attitude change may be congruent — it may change in the same direction as the existing attitude (for example, a positive attitude may become more positive, or a negative attitude may become more negative).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is an incongruent attitude change?
cards.back: On the other hand, an attitude change may be incongruent — it may change in a direction opposite to the existing attitude (for example, a positive attitude becomes less positive, or negative, or a negative attitude becomes less negative, or positive).
cards.quote: On the other hand, an attitude change may be incongruent — it may change in a direction opposite to the existing attitude (for example, a positive attitude becomes less positive, or negative, or a negative attitude becomes less negative, or positive).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which changes are easier to bring about: congruent or incongruent?
cards.back: It has been found that, in general, congruent changes are easier to bring about than are the incongruent changes in attitudes.
cards.quote: It has been found that, in general, congruent changes are easier to bring about than are the incongruent changes in attitudes.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A somewhat positive attitude to women’s empowerment becomes more positive after reading about a successful woman. Congruent or incongruent?
cards.back:
Congruent change
Reading about a successful woman may make this attitude more positive. This would be a congruent change.
cards.quote: Reading about a successful woman may make this attitude more positive. This would be a congruent change.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does research find about using fear to convince people?
cards.back: Research has found that fear sometimes works well in convincing people but if a message generates too much fear, it turns off the receiver and has little persuasive effect.
cards.quote: Research has found that fear sometimes works well in convincing people but if a message generates too much fear, it turns off the receiver and has little persuasive effect.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which two source features affect attitude change?
cards.back: Source credibility and attractiveness are two features that affect attitude change.
cards.quote: Source credibility and attractiveness are two features that affect attitude change.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: From which kind of source are attitudes more likely to change?
cards.back: Attitudes are more likely to change when the message comes from a highly credible source rather than from a low-credible source.
cards.quote: Attitudes are more likely to change when the message comes from a highly credible source rather than from a low-credible source.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the ‘message’ in attitude change?
cards.back: The message is the information that is presented in order to bring about an attitude change.
cards.quote: The message is the information that is presented in order to bring about an attitude change.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How much information about a topic makes attitudes change?
cards.back: Attitudes will change when the amount of information that is given about the topic is just enough, neither too much nor too little.
cards.quote: Attitudes will change when the amount of information that is given about the topic is just enough, neither too much nor too little.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A pressure-cooker advertisement says it saves cooking gas and is economical. Which type of appeal?
cards.back:
Rational appeal
For example, an advertisement for cooking food in a pressure cooker may point out that this saves fuel such as cooking gas (LPG) and is economical (rational appeal).
cards.quote: For example, an advertisement for cooking food in a pressure cooker may point out that this saves fuel such as cooking gas (LPG) and is economical (rational appeal).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A pressure-cooker advertisement says that if one cares for the family, nutrition is a major concern. Which type of appeal?
cards.back:
Emotional appeal
Alternatively, the advertisement may say that pressure-cooking preserves nutrition, and that if one cares for the family, nutrition would be a major concern (emotional appeal)
cards.quote: Alternatively, the advertisement may say that pressure-cooking preserves nutrition, and that if one cares for the family, nutrition would be a major concern (emotional appeal)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which mode of transmitting a message is usually more effective, face-to-face or indirect?
cards.back: Face-to-face transmission of the message is usually more effective than indirect transmission, as for instance, through letters and pamphlets, or even through mass media.
cards.quote: Face-to-face transmission of the message is usually more effective than indirect transmission, as for instance, through letters and pamphlets, or even through mass media.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which qualities of the target influence the likelihood and extent of attitude change?
cards.back: Qualities of the target, such as persuasibility, strong prejudices, self-esteem, and intelligence influence the likelihood and extent of attitude change.
cards.quote: Qualities of the target, such as persuasibility, strong prejudices, self-esteem, and intelligence influence the likelihood and extent of attitude change.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who changes attitudes more easily: persons with low self-esteem or high self-esteem?
cards.back: Persons who have a low self-esteem, and do not have sufficient confidence in themselves, change their attitudes more easily than those who are high on self-esteem.
cards.quote: Persons who have a low self-esteem, and do not have sufficient confidence in themselves, change their attitudes more easily than those who are high on self-esteem.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Are people with strong prejudices more or less prone to attitude change?
cards.back: People with strong prejudices are less prone to any attitude change than those who do not hold strong prejudices.
cards.quote: People with strong prejudices are less prone to any attitude change than those who do not hold strong prejudices.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Do attitudes always show up in behaviour?
cards.back: We usually expect behaviour to follow logically from attitudes. However, an individual’s attitudes may not always be exhibited through behaviour.
cards.quote: We usually expect behaviour to follow logically from attitudes. However, an individual’s attitudes may not always be exhibited through behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which social psychologist asked a Chinese couple to travel across the US and stay in different hotels?
cards.back: Richard LaPiere, an American social psychologist, conducted the following study. He asked a Chinese couple to travel across the United States, and stay in different hotels.
cards.quote: In the days when Americans were said to be prejudiced against the Chinese, Richard LaPiere, an American social psychologist, conducted the following study. He asked a Chinese couple to travel across the United States, and stay in different hotels.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What did LaPiere’s study show about attitudes and actual behaviour?
cards.back: Thus, attitudes may not always predict actual pattern of one’s behaviour.
cards.quote: Thus, attitudes may not always predict actual pattern of one’s behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are prejudices?
cards.back: Prejudices are examples of attitudes towards a particular group. They are usually negative, and in many cases, may be based on stereotypes (the cognitive component) about the specific group.
cards.quote: Prejudices are examples of attitudes towards a particular group. They are usually negative, and in many cases, may be based on stereotypes (the cognitive component) about the specific group.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is discrimination (the behavioural component of prejudice)?
cards.back: Prejudice may also get translated into discrimination, the behavioural component, whereby people behave in a less positive way towards a particular target group compared to another group which they favour.
cards.quote: Prejudice may also get translated into discrimination, the behavioural component, whereby people behave in a less positive way towards a particular target group compared to another group which they favour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which event is an extreme example of prejudice leading to hatred, discrimination and mass killing?
cards.back: The genocide committed by the Nazis in Germany against Jewish people is an extreme example of how prejudice can lead to hatred, discrimination and mass killing of innocent people.
cards.quote: The genocide committed by the Nazis in Germany against Jewish people is an extreme example of how prejudice can lead to hatred, discrimination and mass killing of innocent people.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Can prejudice exist without discrimination, and discrimination without prejudice?
cards.back: Prejudices can exist without being shown in the form of discrimination. Similarly, discrimination can be shown without prejudice.
cards.quote: Prejudices can exist without being shown in the form of discrimination. Similarly, discrimination can be shown without prejudice.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is likely to arise wherever prejudice and discrimination exist?
cards.back: Wherever prejudice and discrimination exist, conflicts are very likely to arise between groups within the same society.
cards.quote: Wherever prejudice and discrimination exist, conflicts are very likely to arise between groups within the same society.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Can law curb discrimination? Which components of prejudice are more difficult to change?
cards.back: Moreover, in many cases discriminatory behaviour can be curbed by law. But, the cognitive and emotional components of prejudice are more difficult to change.
cards.quote: Moreover, in many cases discriminatory behaviour can be curbed by law. But, the cognitive and emotional components of prejudice are more difficult to change.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How can prejudices be learned?
cards.back: Like other attitudes, prejudices can also be learned through association, reward and punishment, observing others, group or cultural norms and exposure to information that encourages prejudice.
cards.quote: Like other attitudes, prejudices can also be learned through association, reward and punishment, observing others, group or cultural norms and exposure to information that encourages prejudice.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What may people who learn prejudiced attitudes develop?
cards.back: People who learn prejudiced attitudes may develop a ‘prejudiced personality’, and show low adjusting capacity, anxiety, and feelings of hostility against the outgroup.
cards.quote: People who learn prejudiced attitudes may develop a ‘prejudiced personality’, and show low adjusting capacity, anxiety, and feelings of hostility against the outgroup.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How does a strong social identity lead to prejudice?
cards.back: Individuals who have a strong sense of social identity and have a very positive attitude towards their own group boost this attitude by holding negative attitudes towards other groups. These are shown as prejudices.
cards.quote: Individuals who have a strong sense of social identity and have a very positive attitude towards their own group boost this attitude by holding negative attitudes towards other groups. These are shown as prejudices.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is scapegoating?
cards.back: Scapegoating : This is a phenomenon by which the majority group places the blame on a minority outgroup for its own social, economic or political problems.
cards.quote: Scapegoating : This is a phenomenon by which the majority group places the blame on a minority outgroup for its own social, economic or political problems.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the ‘kernel of truth’ concept in prejudice?
cards.back: Sometimes people may continue to hold stereotypes because they think that, after all, there must be some truth, or ‘kernel of truth’ in what everyone says about the other group.
cards.quote: Sometimes people may continue to hold stereotypes because they think that, after all, there must be some truth, or ‘kernel of truth’ in what everyone says about the other group.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is a self-fulfilling prophecy as a source of prejudice?
cards.back: In some cases, the group that is the target of prejudice is itself responsible for continuing the prejudice. The target group may behave in ways that justify the prejudice, that is, confirm the negative expectations.
cards.quote: In some cases, the group that is the target of prejudice is itself responsible for continuing the prejudice. The target group may behave in ways that justify the prejudice, that is, confirm the negative expectations.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the first step in handling prejudice?
cards.back: Knowing about the causes or sources would be the first step in handling prejudice.
cards.quote: Knowing about the causes or sources would be the first step in handling prejudice.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is education and information dissemination used for in handling prejudice?
cards.back: Education and information dissemination, for correcting stereotypes related to specific target groups, and tackling the problem of a strong ingroup bias.
cards.quote: Education and information dissemination, for correcting stereotypes related to specific target groups, and tackling the problem of a strong ingroup bias.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does increasing intergroup contact allow for?
cards.back: Increasing intergroup contact allows for direct communication, removal of mistrust between the groups, and even discovery of positive qualities in the outgroup.
cards.quote: Increasing intergroup contact allows for direct communication, removal of mistrust between the groups, and even discovery of positive qualities in the outgroup.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does highlighting individual identity rather than group identity achieve?
cards.back: Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity, thus weakening the importance of group (both ingroup and outgroup) as a basis of evaluating the other person.
cards.quote: Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity, thus weakening the importance of group (both ingroup and outgroup) as a basis of evaluating the other person.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the basic idea of cognitive dissonance about the cognitive components of an attitude?
cards.back: Here the basic idea is that the cognitive components of an attitude must be ‘consonant’ (opposite of ‘dissonant’), i.e., they should be logically in line with each other.
cards.quote: Here the basic idea is that the cognitive components of an attitude must be ‘consonant’ (opposite of ‘dissonant’), i.e., they should be logically in line with each other.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is a stereotype?
cards.back: a stereotype is a cluster of ideas regarding the characteristics of a specific group. All members belonging to this group are assumed to possess these characteristics.
cards.quote: As will be discussed below in the section on social cognition, a stereotype is a cluster of ideas regarding the characteristics of a specific group. All members belonging to this group are assumed to possess these characteristics.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What do stereotypes often consist of, and what do they lead to?
cards.back: Often, stereotypes consist of undesirable characteristics about the target group, and they lead to negative attitudes or prejudices towards members of specific groups.
cards.quote: Often, stereotypes consist of undesirable characteristics about the target group, and they lead to negative attitudes or prejudices towards members of specific groups.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ‘____’ is the term used to describe the level of stress that is good for you
cards.back: ‘Eustress’ is the term used to describe the level of stress that is good for you
cards.quote: ‘Eustress’ is the term used to describe the level of stress that is good for you
cards.note: Good stress; if it turns into distress it causes the body's wear and tear.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Eustress, however, has the potential of turning into ‘____’.
cards.back: Eustress, however, has the potential of turning into ‘distress’.
cards.quote: Eustress, however, has the potential of turning into ‘distress’.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define stress (pattern of responses, NCERT).
cards.back: Thus, stress can be described as the pattern of responses an organism makes to stimulus event that disturbs the equilibrium and exceeds a person's ability to cope.
cards.quote: Thus, stress can be described as the pattern of responses an organism makes to stimulus event that disturbs the equilibrium and exceeds a person's ability to cope.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: From which Latin words does the word 'stress' originate, and what do they mean?
cards.back: The word stress has its origin in the Latin words ‘strictus’, meaning tight or narrow and ‘stringere’, the verb meaning to tighten.
cards.quote: The word stress has its origin in the Latin words ‘strictus’, meaning tight or narrow and ‘stringere’, the verb meaning to tighten.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are stressors?
cards.back: Stressors are events that cause our body to give the stress response.
cards.quote: Stressors are events that cause our body to give the stress response.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The reaction to external stressors is called ‘____’
cards.back: The reaction to external stressors is called ‘strain’
cards.quote: The reaction to external stressors is called ‘strain’

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define stress (Hans Selye).
cards.back: Hans Selye, the father of modern stress research, defined stress as “the nonspecific response of the body to any demand” that is, regardless of the cause of the threat, the individual will respond with the same physiological pattern of reactions.
cards.quote: Hans Selye, the father of modern stress research, defined stress as “the nonspecific response of the body to any demand” that is, regardless of the cause of the threat, the individual will respond with the same physiological pattern of reactions.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How does NCERT describe stress as a dynamic mental or cognitive state?
cards.back: Stress is a dynamic mental/cognitive state. It is a disruption in homeostasis or an imbalance that gives rise to a requirement for resolution of that imbalance or restoration of homeostasis.
cards.quote: Stress is a dynamic mental/cognitive state. It is a disruption in homeostasis or an imbalance that gives rise to a requirement for resolution of that imbalance or restoration of homeostasis.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The perception of stress is dependent upon the individual's cognitive ____ of events and the resources available to deal with them.
cards.back: The perception of stress is dependent upon the individual's cognitive appraisal of events and the resources available to deal with them.
cards.quote: The perception of stress is dependent upon the individual's cognitive appraisal of events and the resources available to deal with them.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The stress process, based on the cognitive theory of stress propounded by ____ and his colleagues, is described in Figure 3.2.
cards.back: The stress process, based on the cognitive theory of stress propounded by Lazarus and his colleagues, is described in Figure 3.2.
cards.quote: The stress process, based on the cognitive theory of stress propounded by Lazarus and his colleagues, is described in Figure 3.2.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is primary appraisal (Lazarus)?
cards.back: Primary appraisal refers to the perception of a new or changing environment as positive, neutral or negative in its consequences.
cards.quote: Primary appraisal refers to the perception of a new or changing environment as positive, neutral or negative in its consequences.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Harm, threat and challenge: how are negative events appraised?
cards.back:
Harm is the assessment of the damage that has already been done by an event.
Threat is the assessment of possible future damage that may be brought about by the event.
Challenge appraisals are associated with more confident expectations of the ability to cope with the stressful event, the potential to overcome and even profit from the event.
cards.quote: Negative events are appraised for their possible harm, threat or challenge. Harm is the assessment of the damage that has already been done by an event. Threat is the assessment of possible future damage that may be brought about by the event. Challenge appraisals are associated with more confident expectations of the ability to cope with the stressful event, the potential to overcome and even profit from the event.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is secondary appraisal?
cards.back: a secondary appraisal, which is the assessment of one's coping abilities and resources and whether they will be sufficient to meet the harm, threat or challenge of the event.
cards.quote: When we perceive an event as stressful, we are likely to make a secondary appraisal, which is the assessment of one's coping abilities and resources and whether they will be sufficient to meet the harm, threat or challenge of the event.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Resources assessed in secondary appraisal: name the four kinds.
cards.back: mental, physical, personal or social
cards.quote: These resources may be mental, physical, personal or social.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress reactions (Fig. 3.2): name the four kinds.
cards.back: physiological, behavioural, emotional, and cognitive
cards.quote: Very often, these stressors result in a variety of stress reactions, which may be physiological, behavioural, emotional, and cognitive

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Physiological stress response: the two pathways started by the hypothalamus.
cards.back:
The first pathway involves the autonomic nervous system. The adrenal gland releases large amount of catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) into the blood stream. This leads to physiological changes seen in fight-or-flight response.
The second pathway involves the pituitary gland, which secretes the corticosteroid (cortisol) which provides energy.
cards.quote: The hypothalamus initiates action along two pathways. The first pathway involves the autonomic nervous system. The adrenal gland releases large amount of catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) into the blood stream. This leads to physiological changes seen in fight-or-flight response. The second pathway involves the pituitary gland, which secretes the corticosteroid (cortisol) which provides energy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Emotional reactions to stress: name the negative emotions NCERT lists.
cards.back: fear, anxiety, embarrassment, anger, depression or even denial
cards.quote: The emotional reactions to experience of stress include negative emotions such as fear, anxiety, embarrassment, anger, depression or even denial.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Confrontative action against the stressor (____) or withdrawal from the threatening event (____)
cards.back: Confrontative action against the stressor (fight) or withdrawal from the threatening event (flight)
cards.quote: Confrontative action against the stressor (fight) or withdrawal from the threatening event (flight)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What do the cognitive responses to stress include?
cards.back: Cognitive responses include beliefs about the harm or threat an event poses and beliefs about its causes or controllability. These include responses such as inability to concentrate, and intrusive, repetitive or morbid thoughts.
cards.quote: Cognitive responses include beliefs about the harm or threat an event poses and beliefs about its causes or controllability. These include responses such as inability to concentrate, and intrusive, repetitive or morbid thoughts.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Dimensions on which the stresses people experience vary (Fig. 3.2).
cards.back:
intensity (low intensity vs. high intensity)
duration (short-term vs. long-term)
complexity (less complex vs. more complex)
predictability (unexpected vs. predictable)
cards.quote: the stresses which people experience also vary in terms of intensity (low intensity vs. high intensity), duration (short-term vs. long-term), complexity (less complex vs. more complex) and predictability (unexpected vs. predictable).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which stresses usually have more negative consequences?
cards.back: Usually more intense, prolonged or chronic, complex and unanticipated stresses have more negative consequences than have less intense, short-term, less complex and expected stresses.
cards.quote: Usually more intense, prolonged or chronic, complex and unanticipated stresses have more negative consequences than have less intense, short-term, less complex and expected stresses.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does the cultural context decide in the experience of stress?
cards.back: The cultural context in which we live determines the meaning of any event and defines the nature of response that is expected under various conditions.
cards.quote: The cultural context in which we live determines the meaning of any event and defines the nature of response that is expected under various conditions.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three major types of stress.
cards.back: physical and environmental, psychological, and social
cards.quote: The three major types of stress, viz. physical and environmental, psychological, and social are listed in Figure 3.2.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are physical stresses?
cards.back: Physical stresses are demands that change the state of our body.
cards.quote: Physical stresses are demands that change the state of our body.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are environmental stresses?
cards.back: Environmental stresses are aspects of our surroundings that are often unavoidable such as air pollution, crowding, noise, heat of the summer, winter cold, etc.
cards.quote: Environmental stresses are aspects of our surroundings that are often unavoidable such as air pollution, crowding, noise, heat of the summer, winter cold, etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is psychological stress?
cards.back: These are stresses that we generate ourselves in our minds. These are personal and unique to the person experiencing them and are internal sources of stress.
cards.quote: These are stresses that we generate ourselves in our minds. These are personal and unique to the person experiencing them and are internal sources of stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Important sources of psychological stress.
cards.back: frustration, conflicts, internal and social pressures
cards.quote: Some of the important sources of psychological stress are frustration, conflicts, internal and social pressures, etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is frustration?
cards.back: Frustration results from the blocking of needs and motives by something or someone that hinders us from achieving a desired goal.
cards.quote: Frustration results from the blocking of needs and motives by something or someone that hinders us from achieving a desired goal.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are conflicts as a source of psychological stress?
cards.back: Conflicts may occur between two or more incompatible needs or motives, e.g. whether to study dance or psychology.
cards.quote: Conflicts may occur between two or more incompatible needs or motives, e.g. whether to study dance or psychology.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are internal pressures?
cards.back: Internal pressures stem from beliefs based upon expectations from inside us to ourselves such as, ‘I must do everything perfectly’.
cards.quote: Internal pressures stem from beliefs based upon expectations from inside us to ourselves such as, ‘I must do everything perfectly’.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are social pressures?
cards.back: Social pressures may be brought about from people who make excessive demands on us.
cards.quote: Social pressures may be brought about from people who make excessive demands on us.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is social stress?
cards.back: These are induced externally and result from our interaction with other people. Social events like death or illness in the family, strained relationships, trouble with neighbours are some examples of social stresses.
cards.quote: These are induced externally and result from our interaction with other people. Social events like death or illness in the family, strained relationships, trouble with neighbours are some examples of social stresses.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the three most important sources of stress.
cards.back:
major stressful life events, such as death of a loved one or personal injury
the annoying frequent hassles of everyday life
traumatic events that affect our lives
cards.quote: Among the most important of these are major stressful life events, such as death of a loved one or personal injury, the annoying frequent hassles of everyday life and traumatic events that affect our lives.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When do life events make us more prone to the symptoms of stress?
cards.back: If several of these life events that are planned (e.g. moving into a new house) or unpredicted (e.g. break-up of a long-term relationship) occur within a short period of time, we find it difficult to cope with them and will be more prone to the symptoms of stress.
cards.quote: If several of these life events that are planned (e.g. moving into a new house) or unpredicted (e.g. break-up of a long-term relationship) occur within a short period of time, we find it difficult to cope with them and will be more prone to the symptoms of stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ____ and ____ developed a life event measure of stress.
cards.back: Holmes and Rahe developed a life event measure of stress.
cards.quote: Holmes and Rahe developed a life event measure of stress.

source.section: A Measure of Stressful Life Events (Box 3.1)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which scale was developed for the Indian population to measure stressful life events, and by whom?
cards.back: A measure of stressful life events based on the above scale known as the Presumptive Stressful Life Events Scale has been developed for the Indian population by Singh, Kaur and Kaur.
cards.quote: A measure of stressful life events based on the above scale known as the Presumptive Stressful Life Events Scale has been developed for the Indian population by Singh, Kaur and Kaur.

source.section: A Measure of Stressful Life Events (Box 3.1)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Scale values of life events: what is the value for the death of one's spouse, and for failure in examination?
cards.back: the death of one's spouse is assigned 95, personal illness or injury 56, failure in examination 43, appearing for examination or interview 43, change in sleeping habits 33
cards.quote: the death of one's spouse is assigned 95, personal illness or injury 56, failure in examination 43, appearing for examination or interview 43, change in sleeping habits 33

source.section: A Measure of Stressful Life Events (Box 3.1)

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are hassles?
cards.back: These are the personal stresses we endure as individuals, due to the happenings in our daily life, such as noisy surroundings, commuting, quarrelsome neighbours, electricity and water shortage, traffic snarls, and so on.
cards.quote: These are the personal stresses we endure as individuals, due to the happenings in our daily life, such as noisy surroundings, commuting, quarrelsome neighbours, electricity and water shortage, traffic snarls, and so on.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are traumatic events?
cards.back: These include being involved in a variety of extreme events such as a fire, train or road accident, robbery, earthquake, tsunami, etc.
cards.quote: These include being involved in a variety of extreme events such as a fire, train or road accident, robbery, earthquake, tsunami, etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How may the effects of traumatic events show up?
cards.back: The effects of these events may occur after some lapse of time and sometimes persist as symptoms of anxiety, flashbacks, dreams and intrusive thoughts, etc.
cards.quote: The effects of these events may occur after some lapse of time and sometimes persist as symptoms of anxiety, flashbacks, dreams and intrusive thoughts, etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the four major effects of stress.
cards.back: emotional, physiological, cognitive, and behavioural
cards.quote: There are four major effects of stress associated with the stressed state, viz. emotional, physiological, cognitive, and behavioural.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are the emotional effects of stress?
cards.back: Those who suffer from stress are far more likely to experience mood swings, and show erratic behaviour that may alienate them from family and friends.
cards.quote: Those who suffer from stress are far more likely to experience mood swings, and show erratic behaviour that may alienate them from family and friends.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which hormones does the body produce more of under stress, and what do they change?
cards.back: it increases the production of certain hormones, such as adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones produce marked changes in heart rate, blood pressure levels, metabolism and physical activity.
cards.quote: it increases the production of certain hormones, such as adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones produce marked changes in heart rate, blood pressure levels, metabolism and physical activity.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Examples of the physiological effects of stress.
cards.back: release of epinephrine and norepinephrine, slowing down of the digestive system, expansion of air passages in the lungs, increased heart rate, and constriction of blood vessels
cards.quote: Examples of physiological effects are release of epinephrine and norepinephrine, slowing down of the digestive system, expansion of air passages in the lungs, increased heart rate, and constriction of blood vessels.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are the cognitive effects of stress?
cards.back: Cognitive effects of stress are poor concentration, and reduced short-term memory capacity.
cards.quote: Cognitive effects of stress are poor concentration, and reduced short-term memory capacity.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Typical behavioural effects of stress.
cards.back: Some of the typical behavioural effects of stress seen are disrupted sleep patterns, increased absenteeism, and reduced work performance.
cards.quote: Some of the typical behavioural effects of stress seen are disrupted sleep patterns, increased absenteeism, and reduced work performance.

source.section: Effects of Stress on Psychological Functioning and Health

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is examination anxiety?
cards.back: Examination anxiety is a fairly common phenomenon that involves feelings of tension or uneasiness that occur before, during, or after an examination.
cards.quote: Examination anxiety is a fairly common phenomenon that involves feelings of tension or uneasiness that occur before, during, or after an examination.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress has been implicated in the development of which disorders?
cards.back: Stress has been implicated in the development of cardiovascular disorders, high blood pressure, as well as psychosomatic disorders including ulcers, asthma, allergies and headaches.
cards.quote: Stress has been implicated in the development of cardiovascular disorders, high blood pressure, as well as psychosomatic disorders including ulcers, asthma, allergies and headaches.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS): the three stages, in order.
cards.back: alarm reaction, resistance, and exhaustion
cards.quote: According to him, GAS involves three stages: alarm reaction, resistance, and exhaustion
cards.note: GAS is Hans Selye's model of the body's response to prolonged stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: GAS stage 1: what happens in the alarm reaction stage?
cards.back: The presence of a noxious stimulus or stressor leads to activation of the adrenal-pituitary-cortex system. This triggers the release of hormones producing the stress response. Now the individual is ready for fight or flight.
cards.quote: Alarm reaction stage : The presence of a noxious stimulus or stressor leads to activation of the adrenal-pituitary-cortex system. This triggers the release of hormones producing the stress response. Now the individual is ready for fight or flight.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: GAS stage 2: what happens in the resistance stage?
cards.back: If stress is prolonged, the resistance stage begins. The parasympathetic nervous system calls for more cautious use of the body's resources. The organism makes efforts to cope with the threat, as through confrontation.
cards.quote: Resistance stage : If stress is prolonged, the resistance stage begins. The parasympathetic nervous system calls for more cautious use of the body's resources. The organism makes efforts to cope with the threat, as through confrontation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: GAS stage 3: what happens in the exhaustion stage?
cards.back: Continued exposure to the same stressor or additional stressors drains the body of its resources and leads to the third stage of exhaustion. The physiological systems involved in alarm reaction and resistance become ineffective and susceptibility to stress-related diseases such as high blood pressure becomes more likely.
cards.quote: Exhaustion stage : Continued exposure to the same stressor or additional stressors drains the body of its resources and leads to the third stage of exhaustion. The physiological systems involved in alarm reaction and resistance become ineffective and susceptibility to stress-related diseases such as high blood pressure becomes more likely.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Selye's model has been criticised for assigning a very limited role to ____ factors in stress.
cards.back: Selye's model has been criticised for assigning a very limited role to psychological factors in stress.
cards.quote: Selye's model has been criticised for assigning a very limited role to psychological factors in stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is psychoneuroimmunology?
cards.back: Psychoneuroimmunology focuses on the links between the mind, the brain and the immune system. It studies the effects of stress on the immune system.
cards.quote: Psychoneuroimmunology focuses on the links between the mind, the brain and the immune system. It studies the effects of stress on the immune system.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What do the white blood cells (leucocytes) of the immune system do?
cards.back: The white blood cells (leucocytes) within the immune system identify and destroy foreign bodies (antigens) such as viruses. It also leads to the production of antibodies.
cards.quote: The white blood cells (leucocytes) within the immune system identify and destroy foreign bodies (antigens) such as viruses. It also leads to the production of antibodies.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Kinds of white blood cells in the immune system and what they do.
cards.back:
T cells destroy invaders, and T-helper cells increase immunological activity.
B cells produce antibodies.
Natural killer cells are involved in the fight against both viruses and tumours.
cards.quote: There are several kinds of white blood cells or leucocytes within the immune system, including T cells, B cells and natural killer cells. T cells destroy invaders, and T-helper cells increase immunological activity. It is these T-helper cells that are attacked by the Human Immuno Deficiency Virus (HIV), the virus causing Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS). B cells produce antibodies. Natural killer cells are involved in the fight against both viruses and tumours.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which immune function does stress affect that defends against infections and cancer?
cards.back: Stress can affect natural killer cell cytotoxicity, which is of major importance in the defence against various infections and cancer.
cards.quote: Stress can affect natural killer cell cytotoxicity, which is of major importance in the defence against various infections and cancer.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who shows better immune functioning according to studies?
cards.back: Studies reveal that immune functioning is better in individuals receiving social support.
cards.quote: Studies reveal that immune functioning is better in individuals receiving social support.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stressed individuals may be more likely to expose themselves to ____, which are agents causing physical illness.
cards.back: Stressed individuals may be more likely to expose themselves to pathogens, which are agents causing physical illness.
cards.quote: Stressed individuals may be more likely to expose themselves to pathogens, which are agents causing physical illness.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which health promoting behaviours play an important role in good health?
cards.back: Studies have revealed that health promoting behaviour like balanced diet, regular exercise, family support, etc. play an important role in good health.
cards.quote: Studies have revealed that health promoting behaviour like balanced diet, regular exercise, family support, etc. play an important role in good health.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define coping.
cards.back: Coping is a dynamic situation-specific reaction to stress. It is a set of concrete responses to stressful situations or events that are intended to resolve the problem and reduce stress.
cards.quote: Coping is a dynamic situation-specific reaction to stress. It is a set of concrete responses to stressful situations or events that are intended to resolve the problem and reduce stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Task-oriented coping strategy (Endler and Parker).
cards.back: This involves obtaining information about the stressful situation and about alternative courses of action and their probable outcome; it also involves deciding priorities and acting so as to deal directly with the stressful situation.
cards.quote: Task-oriented Strategy : This involves obtaining information about the stressful situation and about alternative courses of action and their probable outcome; it also involves deciding priorities and acting so as to deal directly with the stressful situation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Emotion-oriented coping strategy (Endler and Parker).
cards.back: This can involve efforts to maintain hope and to control one's emotions; it can also involve venting feelings of anger and frustration, or deciding that nothing can be done to change things.
cards.quote: Emotion-oriented Strategy : This can involve efforts to maintain hope and to control one's emotions; it can also involve venting feelings of anger and frustration, or deciding that nothing can be done to change things.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Endler and Parker: the three main types of coping.
cards.back: task-oriented, emotion-oriented, and avoidance-oriented coping
cards.quote: There are three main types of coping, task-oriented, emotion-oriented, and avoidance-oriented coping.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Lazarus and Folkman has conceptualised coping as a dynamic process rather than an individual ____.
cards.back: Lazarus and Folkman has conceptualised coping as a dynamic process rather than an individual trait.
cards.quote: Lazarus and Folkman has conceptualised coping as a dynamic process rather than an individual trait.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define coping (Lazarus and Folkman).
cards.back: Coping refers to constantly changing cognitive and behavioural efforts to master, reduce or tolerate the internal or external demands that are created by the stressful transaction.
cards.quote: Coping refers to constantly changing cognitive and behavioural efforts to master, reduce or tolerate the internal or external demands that are created by the stressful transaction.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Lazarus and Folkman: the two types of coping responses.
cards.back: problem-focused and emotion-focused
cards.quote: According to them coping responses can be divided into two types of responses, problem-focused and emotion-focused.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are problem-focused coping strategies?
cards.back: Problem-focused strategies attack the problem itself, with behaviours designed to gain information, to alter the event, and to alter belief and commitments.
cards.quote: Problem-focused strategies attack the problem itself, with behaviours designed to gain information, to alter the event, and to alter belief and commitments. They increase the person's awareness, level of knowledge, and range of behavioural and cognitive coping options. They can act to reduce the threat value of the event.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are emotion-focused coping strategies?
cards.back: Emotion-focused strategies call for psychological changes designed primarily to limit the degree of emotional disruption caused by an event, with minimal effort to alter the event itself.
cards.quote: Emotion-focused strategies call for psychological changes designed primarily to limit the degree of emotional disruption caused by an event, with minimal effort to alter the event itself.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which coping do people generally use more often, problem-focused or emotion-focused?
cards.back: While both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping are necessary when facing stressful situations, research suggests that people generally tend to use the former more often than the latter.
cards.quote: While both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping are necessary when facing stressful situations, research suggests that people generally tend to use the former more often than the latter.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which illnesses are linked to stress ("Stress is a silent killer")?
cards.back: Stress is a silent killer. It is estimated to play a significant role in physical illness and disease. Hypertension, heart disease, ulcers, diabetes and even cancer are linked to stress.
cards.quote: Stress is a silent killer. It is estimated to play a significant role in physical illness and disease. Hypertension, heart disease, ulcers, diabetes and even cancer are linked to stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is relaxation as a stress management technique?
cards.back: It is an active skill that reduces symptoms of stress and decreases the incidence of illnesses such as high blood pressure and heart disease.
cards.quote: Relaxation Techniques : It is an active skill that reduces symptoms of stress and decreases the incidence of illnesses such as high blood pressure and heart disease.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the yogic method of meditation?
cards.back: The yogic method of meditation consists of a sequence of learned techniques for refocusing of attention that brings about an altered state of consciousness.
cards.quote: Meditation Procedures : The yogic method of meditation consists of a sequence of learned techniques for refocusing of attention that brings about an altered state of consciousness.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is biofeedback?
cards.back: It is a procedure to monitor and reduce the physiological aspects of stress by providing feedback about current physiological activity and is often accompanied by relaxation training.
cards.quote: Biofeedback : It is a procedure to monitor and reduce the physiological aspects of stress by providing feedback about current physiological activity and is often accompanied by relaxation training.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Biofeedback training: the three stages, in order.
cards.back:
developing an awareness of the particular physiological response, e.g. heart rate
learning ways of controlling that physiological response in quiet conditions
transferring that control into the conditions of everyday life
cards.quote: Biofeedback training involves three stages : developing an awareness of the particular physiological response, e.g. heart rate, learning ways of controlling that physiological response in quiet conditions; and transferring that control into the conditions of everyday life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is creative visualisation?
cards.back: Creative visualisation is a subjective experience that uses imagery and imagination.
cards.quote: Creative visualisation is a subjective experience that uses imagery and imagination.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress inoculation training (Meichenbaum): what is the essence of the approach?
cards.back: Stress inoculation training is one effective method developed by Meichenbaum. The essence of this approach is to replace negative and irrational thoughts with positive and rational ones.
cards.quote: Stress inoculation training is one effective method developed by Meichenbaum. The essence of this approach is to replace negative and irrational thoughts with positive and rational ones.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress inoculation training: the three main phases, in order.
cards.back: assessment, stress reduction techniques, and application and follow-through
cards.quote: There are three main phases in this : assessment, stress reduction techniques, and application and follow-through.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In stress inoculation training, what does the assessment phase involve?
cards.back: Assessment involves discussing the nature of the problem and seeing it from the viewpoint of the person/client.
cards.quote: Assessment involves discussing the nature of the problem and seeing it from the viewpoint of the person/client.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How does exercise help with stress?
cards.back: Exercise can provide an active outlet for the physiological arousal experienced in response to stress.
cards.quote: Exercise can provide an active outlet for the physiological arousal experienced in response to stress.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: One must practice these exercises at least ____ times a week for ____ minutes at a time.
cards.back: One must practice these exercises at least four times a week for 30 minutes at a time.
cards.quote: One must practice these exercises at least four times a week for 30 minutes at a time.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Kobasa: which people share the personality traits of hardiness?
cards.back: Recent studies by Kobasa have shown that people with high levels of stress but low levels of illness share three characteristics, which are referred to as the personality traits of hardiness.
cards.quote: Recent studies by Kobasa have shown that people with high levels of stress but low levels of illness share three characteristics, which are referred to as the personality traits of hardiness.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Hardiness (Kobasa): what are the three Cs?
cards.back: commitment, control, and challenge
cards.quote: It consists of ‘the three Cs’, i.e. commitment, control, and challenge.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is hardiness?
cards.back: Hardiness is a set of beliefs about oneself, the world, and how they interact.
cards.quote: Hardiness is a set of beliefs about oneself, the world, and how they interact.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Stress resistant personality: what do control, commitment and challenge mean?
cards.back: Stress resistant personalities have control which is a sense of purpose and direction in life; commitment to work, family, hobbies and social life; and challenge, that is, they see changes in life as normal and positive rather than as a threat.
cards.quote: Stress resistant personalities have control which is a sense of purpose and direction in life; commitment to work, family, hobbies and social life; and challenge, that is, they see changes in life as normal and positive rather than as a threat.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define life skills.
cards.back: Life skills are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life.
cards.quote: Life skills are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the life skills NCERT lists for meeting the challenges of life.
cards.back: Assertiveness, time management, rational thinking, improving relationships, self-care, and overcoming unhelpful habits such as perfectionism, procrastination
cards.quote: Assertiveness, time management, rational thinking, improving relationships, self-care, and overcoming unhelpful habits such as perfectionism, procrastination, etc. are some life skills that will help to meet the challenges of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is assertiveness?
cards.back: Assertiveness is a behaviour or skill that helps to communicate, clearly and confidently, our feelings, needs, wants, and thoughts.
cards.quote: Assertiveness is a behaviour or skill that helps to communicate, clearly and confidently, our feelings, needs, wants, and thoughts.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does assertiveness let you do?
cards.back: It is the ability to say no to a request, to state an opinion without being self-conscious, or to express emotions such as love, anger, etc. openly.
cards.quote: It is the ability to say no to a request, to state an opinion without being self-conscious, or to express emotions such as love, anger, etc. openly.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the central principle of time management?
cards.back: The central principle of time management is to spend your time doing the things that you value, or that help you to achieve your goals.
cards.quote: The central principle of time management is to spend your time doing the things that you value, or that help you to achieve your goals.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Some principles of rational thinking.
cards.back: challenging your distorted thinking and irrational beliefs, driving out potentially intrusive negative anxiety-provoking thoughts, and making positive statements
