cards.quote: The therapist encourages this by being accepting, empathic, genuine and warm to the client.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Sympathy vs intellectual understanding vs empathy: the difference.
cards.back: In sympathy, one has compassion and pity towards the suffering of another but is not able to feel like the other person. Intellectual understanding is cold in the sense that the person is unable to feel like the other person and does not feel sympathy either. On the other hand, empathy is present when one is able to understand the plight of another person, and feel like the other person.
cards.quote: In sympathy, one has compassion and pity towards the suffering of another but is not able to feel like the other person. Intellectual understanding is cold in the sense that the person is unable to feel like the other person and does not feel sympathy either. On the other hand, empathy is present when one is able to understand the plight of another person, and feel like the other person.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is empathy?
cards.back: On the other hand, empathy is present when one is able to understand the plight of another person, and feel like the other person. It means understanding things from the other person's perspective, i.e. putting oneself in the other person's shoes.
cards.quote: On the other hand, empathy is present when one is able to understand the plight of another person, and feel like the other person. It means understanding things from the other person's perspective, i.e. putting oneself in the other person's shoes.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Empathy enriches the therapeutic relationship and transforms it into a ____ relationship.
cards.back: Empathy enriches the therapeutic relationship and transforms it into a healing relationship.
cards.quote: Empathy enriches the therapeutic relationship and transforms it into a healing relationship.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Types of psychotherapies (three broad groups).
cards.back:
the psychodynamic
behaviour
existential psychotherapies
cards.quote: Psychotherapies may be classified into three broad groups, viz. the psychodynamic, behaviour, and existential psychotherapies.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In what order did psychodynamic, behaviour and existential therapies emerge? Which is called the third force?
cards.back: In terms of the chronological order, psychodynamic therapy emerged first followed by behaviour therapy while the existential therapies which are also called the third force, emerged last.
cards.quote: In terms of the chronological order, psychodynamic therapy emerged first followed by behaviour therapy while the existential therapies which are also called the third force, emerged last.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychodynamic vs behaviour vs existential therapies: the difference on the cause of the problem.
cards.back: Psychodynamic therapy is of the view that intrapsychic conflicts, i.e. the conflicts that are present within the psyche of the person, are the source of psychological problems. According to behaviour therapies, psychological problems arise due to faulty learning of behaviours and cognitions. The existential therapies postulate that the questions about the meaning of one's life and existence are the cause of psychological problems.
cards.quote: Psychodynamic therapy is of the view that intrapsychic conflicts, i.e. the conflicts that are present within the psyche of the person, are the source of psychological problems. According to behaviour therapies, psychological problems arise due to faulty learning of behaviours and cognitions. The existential therapies postulate that the questions about the meaning of one's life and existence are the cause of psychological problems.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychodynamic vs behaviour therapy: the difference on how the cause came into existence.
cards.back: In the psychodynamic therapy, unfulfilled desires of childhood and unresolved childhood fears lead to intrapsychic conflicts. The behaviour therapy postulates that faulty conditioning patterns, faulty learning, and faulty thinking and beliefs lead to maladaptive behaviours that, in turn, lead to psychological problems.
cards.quote: In the psychodynamic therapy, unfulfilled desires of childhood and unresolved childhood fears lead to intrapsychic conflicts. The behaviour therapy postulates that faulty conditioning patterns, faulty learning, and faulty thinking and beliefs lead to maladaptive behaviours that, in turn, lead to psychological problems.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The existential therapy places importance on the ____.
cards.back: The existential therapy places importance on the present.
cards.quote: The existential therapy places importance on the present.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychodynamic vs behaviour therapy: the difference on the chief method of treatment.
cards.back: Psychodynamic therapy uses the methods of free association and reporting of dreams to elicit the thoughts and feelings of the client. This material is interpreted to the client to help her/him to confront and resolve the conflicts and thus overcome problems. Behaviour therapy identifies the faulty conditioning patterns and sets up alternate behavioural contingencies to improve behaviour.
cards.quote: Psychodynamic therapy uses the methods of free association and reporting of dreams to elicit the thoughts and feelings of the client. This material is interpreted to the client to help her/him to confront and resolve the conflicts and thus overcome problems. Behaviour therapy identifies the faulty conditioning patterns and sets up alternate behavioural contingencies to improve behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The existential therapy provides a therapeutic environment which is positive, accepting, and ____.
cards.back: The existential therapy provides a therapeutic environment which is positive, accepting, and nonjudgmental.
cards.quote: The existential therapy provides a therapeutic environment which is positive, accepting, and nonjudgmental.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychodynamic and behaviour vs existential therapies: the difference on the therapist's role.
cards.back: Both the psychodynamic and the behaviour therapies assume that the therapist is capable of arriving at solutions to the client's problems. In contrast to these therapies, the existential therapies emphasise that the therapist merely provides a warm, empathic relationship in which the client feels secure to explore the nature and causes of her/his problems by herself/himself.
cards.quote: Both the psychodynamic and the behaviour therapies assume that the therapist is capable of arriving at solutions to the client's problems. In contrast to these therapies, the existential therapies emphasise that the therapist merely provides a warm, empathic relationship in which the client feels secure to explore the nature and causes of her/his problems by herself/himself.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychodynamic therapy values ____ as the important benefit that the client derives from the treatment.
cards.back: Psychodynamic therapy values emotional insight as the important benefit that the client derives from the treatment.
cards.quote: Psychodynamic therapy values emotional insight as the important benefit that the client derives from the treatment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When is emotional insight present?
cards.back: Emotional insight is present when the client understands her/his conflicts intellectually; is able to accept the same emotionally; and is able to change her/his emotions towards the conflicts.
cards.quote: Emotional insight is present when the client understands her/his conflicts intellectually; is able to accept the same emotionally; and is able to change her/his emotions towards the conflicts.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The behaviour therapy considers changing faulty behaviour and thought patterns to ____ ones as the chief benefit of the treatment.
cards.back: The behaviour therapy considers changing faulty behaviour and thought patterns to adaptive ones as the chief benefit of the treatment.
cards.quote: The behaviour therapy considers changing faulty behaviour and thought patterns to adaptive ones as the chief benefit of the treatment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The humanistic therapy values ____ as the chief benefit.
cards.back: The humanistic therapy values personal growth as the chief benefit.
cards.quote: The humanistic therapy values personal growth as the chief benefit.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is personal growth?
cards.back: Personal growth is the process of gaining increasing understanding of oneself, and one's aspirations, emotions and motives.
cards.quote: Personal growth is the process of gaining increasing understanding of oneself, and one's aspirations, emotions and motives.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychoanalysis vs behaviour/existential therapies: the difference on duration of treatment.
cards.back: The duration of classical psychoanalysis may continue for several years. However, several recent versions of psychodynamic therapies are completed in 10-15 sessions. Behaviour and cognitive behaviour therapies as well as existential therapies are shorter and are completed in a few months.
cards.quote: The duration of classical psychoanalysis may continue for several years. However, several recent versions of psychodynamic therapies are completed in 10-15 sessions. Behaviour and cognitive behaviour therapies as well as existential therapies are shorter and are completed in a few months.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is clinical formulation?
cards.back: Clinical formulation refers to formulating the problem of the client in the therapeutic model being used for the treatment.
cards.quote: Clinical formulation refers to formulating the problem of the client in the therapeutic model being used for the treatment.

source.section: Steps in the Formulation of a Client's Problem

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Behaviour therapies postulate that psychological distress arises because of ____ behaviour patterns or thought patterns.
cards.back: Behaviour therapies postulate that psychological distress arises because of faulty behaviour patterns or thought patterns.
cards.quote: Behaviour therapies postulate that psychological distress arises because of faulty behaviour patterns or thought patterns.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define behaviour therapy.
cards.back: The clinical application of learning theory principles constitute behaviour therapy.
cards.quote: The clinical application of learning theory principles constitute behaviour therapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does behavioural analysis find? Name the 3 things.
cards.back:
malfunctioning behaviours
the antecedents of faulty learning
the factors that maintain or continue faulty learning
cards.quote: Behavioural analysis is conducted to find malfunctioning behaviours, the antecedents of faulty learning, and the factors that maintain or continue faulty learning.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are malfunctioning behaviours?
cards.back: Malfunctioning behaviours are those behaviours which cause distress to the client.
cards.quote: Malfunctioning behaviours are those behaviours which cause distress to the client.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are antecedent factors in behavioural analysis?
cards.back: Antecedent factors are those causes which predispose the person to indulge in that behaviour.
cards.quote: Antecedent factors are those causes which predispose the person to indulge in that behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are maintaining factors in behavioural analysis?
cards.back: Maintaining factors are those factors which lead to the persistence of the faulty behaviour.
cards.quote: Maintaining factors are those factors which lead to the persistence of the faulty behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What do antecedent operations do?
cards.back: Antecedent operations control behaviour by changing something that precedes such a behaviour.
cards.quote: Antecedent operations control behaviour by changing something that precedes such a behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is an establishing operation?
cards.back: The change can be done by increasing or decreasing the reinforcing value of a particular consequence. This is called establishing operation.
cards.quote: The change can be done by increasing or decreasing the reinforcing value of a particular consequence. This is called establishing operation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the two major techniques of behaviour modification.
cards.back:
Negative reinforcement
aversive conditioning
cards.quote: Negative reinforcement and aversive conditioning are the two major techniques of behaviour modification.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What provides negative reinforcement?
cards.back: responses that lead organisms to get rid of painful stimuli or avoid and escape from them provide negative reinforcement.
cards.quote: responses that lead organisms to get rid of painful stimuli or avoid and escape from them provide negative reinforcement.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define aversive conditioning.
cards.back: Aversive conditioning refers to repeated association of undesired response with an aversive consequence.
cards.quote: Aversive conditioning refers to repeated association of undesired response with an aversive consequence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: An alcoholic is given a mild electric shock and asked to smell the alcohol. Which technique is this?
cards.back:
Aversive conditioning
For example, an alcoholic is given a mild electric shock and asked to smell the alcohol. With repeated pairings the smell of alcohol is aversive as the pain of the shock is associated with it and the person will give up alcohol.
cards.quote: For example, an alcoholic is given a mild electric shock and asked to smell the alcohol. With repeated pairings the smell of alcohol is aversive as the pain of the shock is associated with it and the person will give up alcohol.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: If an adaptive behaviour occurs rarely, ____ is given to increase the deficit.
cards.back: If an adaptive behaviour occurs rarely, positive reinforcement is given to increase the deficit.
cards.quote: If an adaptive behaviour occurs rarely, positive reinforcement is given to increase the deficit.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is token economy?
cards.back: Persons with behavioural problems can be given a token as a reward every time a wanted behaviour occurs. The tokens are collected and exchanged for a reward such as an outing for the patient or a treat for the child. This is known as token economy.
cards.quote: Persons with behavioural problems can be given a token as a reward every time a wanted behaviour occurs. The tokens are collected and exchanged for a reward such as an outing for the patient or a treat for the child. This is known as token economy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Unwanted behaviour can be reduced and wanted behaviour can be increased simultaneously through ____.
cards.back: Unwanted behaviour can be reduced and wanted behaviour can be increased simultaneously through differential reinforcement.
cards.quote: Unwanted behaviour can be reduced and wanted behaviour can be increased simultaneously through differential reinforcement.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Two methods of differential reinforcement.
cards.back:
Positive reinforcement for the wanted behaviour and negative reinforcement for the unwanted behaviour attempted together
to positively reinforce the wanted behaviour and ignore the unwanted behaviour
cards.quote: Positive reinforcement for the wanted behaviour and negative reinforcement for the unwanted behaviour attempted together may be one such method. The other method is to positively reinforce the wanted behaviour and ignore the unwanted behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is systematic desensitisation (introduced by whom)?
cards.back: Systematic desensitisation is a technique introduced by Wolpe for treating phobias or irrational fears.
cards.quote: Systematic desensitisation is a technique introduced by Wolpe for treating phobias or irrational fears.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: State the principle of reciprocal inhibition.
cards.back: This principle states that the presence of two mutually opposing forces at the same time, inhibits the weaker force.
cards.quote: This principle states that the presence of two mutually opposing forces at the same time, inhibits the weaker force.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is modelling in behaviour therapy?
cards.back: Modelling is the procedure wherein the client learns to behave in a certain way by observing the behaviour of a role model or the therapist who initially acts as the role model.
cards.quote: Modelling is the procedure wherein the client learns to behave in a certain way by observing the behaviour of a role model or the therapist who initially acts as the role model.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ____, i.e. learning by observing others, is used and through a process of rewarding small changes in the behaviour
cards.back: Vicarious learning, i.e. learning by observing others, is used and through a process of rewarding small changes in the behaviour
cards.quote: Vicarious learning, i.e. learning by observing others, is used and through a process of rewarding small changes in the behaviour

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The skill of the therapist lies in conducting an accurate ____ and building a treatment package with the appropriate techniques.
cards.back: The skill of the therapist lies in conducting an accurate behavioural analysis and building a treatment package with the appropriate techniques.
cards.quote: The skill of the therapist lies in conducting an accurate behavioural analysis and building a treatment package with the appropriate techniques.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Cognitive therapies locate the cause of psychological distress in ____ thoughts and beliefs.
cards.back: Cognitive therapies locate the cause of psychological distress in irrational thoughts and beliefs.
cards.quote: Cognitive therapies locate the cause of psychological distress in irrational thoughts and beliefs.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who formulated Rational Emotive Therapy (RET), and what is its central thesis?
cards.back: Albert Ellis formulated the Rational Emotive Therapy (RET). The central thesis of this therapy is that irrational beliefs mediate between the antecedent events and their consequences.
cards.quote: Albert Ellis formulated the Rational Emotive Therapy (RET). The central thesis of this therapy is that irrational beliefs mediate between the antecedent events and their consequences.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the first step in RET?
cards.back: The first step in RET is the antecedent-belief-consequence (ABC) analysis.
cards.quote: The first step in RET is the antecedent-belief-consequence (ABC) analysis.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What kind of thoughts characterise irrational beliefs in RET?
cards.back: These beliefs are characterised by thoughts with 'musts' and 'shoulds', i.e. things 'must' and 'should' be in a particular manner.
cards.quote: These beliefs are characterised by thoughts with 'musts' and 'shoulds', i.e. things 'must' and 'should' be in a particular manner.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which kind of belief is "One should be loved by everybody all the time"?
cards.back:
An irrational belief (RET)
Examples of irrational beliefs are, "One should be loved by everybody all the time", "Human misery is caused by external events over which one does not have any control", etc.
cards.quote: Examples of irrational beliefs are, "One should be loved by everybody all the time", "Human misery is caused by external events over which one does not have any control", etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In the process of RET, the irrational beliefs are ____ by the therapist through a process of non-directive questioning.
cards.back: In the process of RET, the irrational beliefs are refuted by the therapist through a process of non-directive questioning.
cards.quote: In the process of RET, the irrational beliefs are refuted by the therapist through a process of non-directive questioning.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Beck's account, a client neglected by parents as a child develops which core schema?
cards.back:
The core schema of "I am not wanted"
Thus, a client, who was neglected by the parents as a child, develops the core schema of "I am not wanted".
cards.quote: Thus, a client, who was neglected by the parents as a child, develops the core schema of "I am not wanted".

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are negative (automatic) thoughts in Beck's cognitive therapy?
cards.back: Negative thoughts are persistent irrational thoughts such as "nobody loves me", "I am ugly", "I am stupid", "I will not succeed", etc.
cards.quote: Negative thoughts are persistent irrational thoughts such as "nobody loves me", "I am ugly", "I am stupid", "I will not succeed", etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define cognitive distortions.
cards.back: Cognitive distortions are ways of thinking which are general in nature but which distort the reality in a negative manner.
cards.quote: Cognitive distortions are ways of thinking which are general in nature but which distort the reality in a negative manner.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The therapist uses questioning, which is gentle, non-threatening ____ of the client's beliefs and thoughts.
cards.back: The therapist uses questioning, which is gentle, non-threatening disputation of the client's beliefs and thoughts.
cards.quote: The therapist uses questioning, which is gentle, non-threatening disputation of the client's beliefs and thoughts.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The most popular therapy presently is the ____ (CBT).
cards.back: The most popular therapy presently is the Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT).
cards.quote: The most popular therapy presently is the Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)?
cards.back: CBT adopts a bio-psychosocial approach to the delineation of psychopathology. It combines cognitive therapy with behavioural techniques.
cards.quote: CBT adopts a bio-psychosocial approach to the delineation of psychopathology. It combines cognitive therapy with behavioural techniques.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: CBT is a short and efficacious treatment for which disorders (NCERT's list)?
cards.back:
anxiety
depression
panic attacks
borderline personality
cards.quote: Research into the outcome and effectiveness of psychotherapy has conclusively established CBT to be a short and efficacious treatment for a wide range of psychological disorders such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, and borderline personality, etc.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define self-actualisation.
cards.back: Self-actualisation is defined as an innate or inborn force that moves the person to become more complex, balanced, and integrated, i.e. achieving the complexity and balance without being fragmented.
cards.quote: Self-actualisation is defined as an innate or inborn force that moves the person to become more complex, balanced, and integrated, i.e. achieving the complexity and balance without being fragmented.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does 'integrated' mean (in self-actualisation)?
cards.back: Integrated means a sense of whole, being a complete person, being in essence the same person in spite of the variety of experiences that one is subjected to.
cards.quote: Integrated means a sense of whole, being a complete person, being in essence the same person in spite of the variety of experiences that one is subjected to.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Healing occurs when the client is able to perceive the ____ to self-actualisation in her/his life and is able to remove them.
cards.back: Healing occurs when the client is able to perceive the obstacles to self-actualisation in her/his life and is able to remove them.
cards.quote: Healing occurs when the client is able to perceive the obstacles to self-actualisation in her/his life and is able to remove them.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In humanistic-existential therapy, what is the therapist's role?
cards.back: The therapist is merely a facilitator and guide.
cards.quote: The therapist is merely a facilitator and guide.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who propounded Logotherapy, and what does it mean?
cards.back: Victor Frankl, a psychiatrist and neurologist propounded the Logotherapy. Logos is the Greek word for soul and Logotherapy means treatment for the soul.
cards.quote: Victor Frankl, a psychiatrist and neurologist propounded the Logotherapy. Logos is the Greek word for soul and Logotherapy means treatment for the soul.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Frankl calls this process of finding meaning even in life-threatening circumstances as the process of ____.
cards.back: Frankl calls this process of finding meaning even in life-threatening circumstances as the process of meaning making.
cards.quote: Frankl calls this process of finding meaning even in life-threatening circumstances as the process of meaning making.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Logotherapy, what is actively discouraged?
cards.back: Transference is actively discouraged.
cards.quote: Transference is actively discouraged.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who gave client-centred therapy?
cards.back: Client-centred therapy was given by Carl Rogers.
cards.quote: Client-centred therapy was given by Carl Rogers.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is unconditional positive regard?
cards.back: Unconditional positive regard indicates that the positive warmth of the therapist is not dependent on what the client reveals or does in the therapy sessions.
cards.quote: Unconditional positive regard indicates that the positive warmth of the therapist is not dependent on what the client reveals or does in the therapy sessions.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does 'gestalt' mean, and who gave Gestalt therapy?
cards.back: The German word gestalt means 'whole'. This therapy was given by Freiderick (Fritz) Perls together with his wife Laura Perls.
cards.quote: The German word gestalt means 'whole'. This therapy was given by Freiderick (Fritz) Perls together with his wife Laura Perls.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The goal of gestalt therapy is to increase an individual's ____ and ____.
cards.back: The goal of gestalt therapy is to increase an individual's self-awareness and self-acceptance.
cards.quote: The goal of gestalt therapy is to increase an individual's self-awareness and self-acceptance.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Why are some healing factors called non-specific?
cards.back: These factors are called non-specific because they occur across different systems of psychotherapy and across different clients/patients and different therapists.
cards.quote: These factors are called non-specific because they occur across different systems of psychotherapy and across different clients/patients and different therapists.

source.section: Factors Contributing to Healing in Psychotherapy

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Patient variables vs therapist variables (non-specific factors).
cards.back: Non-specific factors attributable to the client/patient are motivation for change, expectation of improvement due to the treatment, etc. These are called patient variables. Non-specific factors attributable to the therapist are positive nature, absence of unresolved emotional conflicts, presence of good mental health, etc. These are called therapist variables.
cards.quote: Non-specific factors attributable to the client/patient are motivation for change, expectation of improvement due to the treatment, etc. These are called patient variables. Non-specific factors attributable to the therapist are positive nature, absence of unresolved emotional conflicts, presence of good mental health, etc. These are called therapist variables.

source.section: Factors Contributing to Healing in Psychotherapy

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the 6 ethical standards for professional psychotherapists.
cards.back:
Informed consent needs to be taken.
Confidentiality of the client should be maintained.
Alleviating personal distress and suffering should be the goal of all attempts of the therapist.
Integrity of the practitioner-client relationship is important.
Respect for human rights and dignity.
Professional competence and skills are essential.
cards.quote: Some of the ethical standards that need to be practiced by professional psychotherapists are : 1. Informed consent needs to be taken. 2. Confidentiality of the client should be maintained. 3. Alleviating personal distress and suffering should be the goal of all attempts of the therapist. 4. Integrity of the practitioner-client relationship is important. 5. Respect for human rights and dignity. 6. Professional competence and skills are essential.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Why are alternative therapies so called?
cards.back: Alternative therapies are so called, because they are alternative treatment possibilities to the conventional drug treatment or psychotherapy.
cards.quote: Alternative therapies are so called, because they are alternative treatment possibilities to the conventional drug treatment or psychotherapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the alternative therapies NCERT lists.
cards.back:
yoga
meditation
acupuncture
herbal remedies
cards.quote: There are many alternative therapies such as yoga, meditation, acupuncture, herbal remedies and so on.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Yoga is an ancient Indian technique detailed in the Ashtanga Yoga of ____ Yoga Sutras.
cards.back: Yoga is an ancient Indian technique detailed in the Ashtanga Yoga of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.
cards.quote: Yoga is an ancient Indian technique detailed in the Ashtanga Yoga of Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Yoga as it is commonly called today either refers to only the asanas or body posture component or to breathing practices or ____
cards.back: Yoga as it is commonly called today either refers to only the asanas or body posture component or to breathing practices or pranayama
cards.quote: Yoga as it is commonly called today either refers to only the asanas or body posture component or to breathing practices or pranayama

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is meditation?
cards.back: Meditation refers to the practice of focusing attention on breath or on an object or thought or a mantra.
cards.quote: Meditation refers to the practice of focusing attention on breath or on an object or thought or a mantra.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is Vipasana (mindfulness-based) meditation?
cards.back: In Vipasana meditation, also known as mindfulness-based meditation, there is no fixed object or thought to hold the attention. The person passively observes the various bodily sensations and thoughts that are passing through in her or his awareness.
cards.quote: In Vipasana meditation, also known as mindfulness-based meditation, there is no fixed object or thought to hold the attention. The person passively observes the various bodily sensations and thoughts that are passing through in her or his awareness.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The rapid breathing techniques to induce hyperventilation as in ____ (SKY) is found to be a beneficial, low-risk, low-cost adjunct
cards.back: The rapid breathing techniques to induce hyperventilation as in Sudarshana Kriya Yoga (SKY) is found to be a beneficial, low-risk, low-cost adjunct
cards.quote: The rapid breathing techniques to induce hyperventilation as in Sudarshana Kriya Yoga (SKY) is found to be a beneficial, low-risk, low-cost adjunct

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Yoga techniques enhance which five things (NCERT's list)?
cards.back:
well-being
mood
attention
mental focus
stress tolerance
cards.quote: Yoga techniques enhance well-being, mood, attention, mental focus, and stress tolerance.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Proper training by a skilled teacher and a ____ practice every day will maximise the benefits.
cards.back: Proper training by a skilled teacher and a 30-minute practice every day will maximise the benefits.
cards.quote: Proper training by a skilled teacher and a 30-minute practice every day will maximise the benefits.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What did NIMHANS research show about SKY?
cards.back: Research conducted at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), India, has shown that SKY reduces depression.
cards.quote: Research conducted at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), India, has shown that SKY reduces depression.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does Kundalini Yoga combine?
cards.back: Kundalini Yoga combines pranayama or breathing techniques with chanting of mantras.
cards.quote: Kundalini Yoga combines pranayama or breathing techniques with chanting of mantras.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Kundalini Yoga was found effective in the treatment of which disorder (Institute for Nonlinear Science, UC San Diego)?
cards.back: The Institute for Nonlinear Science, University of California, San Diego, USA has found that Kundalini Yoga is effective in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
cards.quote: The Institute for Nonlinear Science, University of California, San Diego, USA has found that Kundalini Yoga is effective in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Prevention of repeated episodes of depression may be helped by mindfulness-based meditation or ____.
cards.back: Prevention of repeated episodes of depression may be helped by mindfulness-based meditation or Vipasana.
cards.quote: Prevention of repeated episodes of depression may be helped by mindfulness-based meditation or Vipasana.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the two components of the treatment of psychological disorders.
cards.back:
reduction of symptoms
improving the level of functioning or quality of life
cards.quote: The treatment of psychological disorders has two components, i.e. reduction of symptoms, and improving the level of functioning or quality of life.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the 3 therapies given in rehabilitation.
cards.back:
occupational therapy
social skills training
vocational therapy
cards.quote: In rehabilitation, the patients are given occupational therapy, social skills training, and vocational therapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In occupational therapy, the patients are taught skills such as candle making, paper bag making and weaving to help them to form a ____.
cards.back: In occupational therapy, the patients are taught skills such as candle making, paper bag making and weaving to help them to form a work discipline.
cards.quote: In occupational therapy, the patients are taught skills such as candle making, paper bag making and weaving to help them to form a work discipline.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Social skills training helps the patients to develop ____ through role play, imitation and instruction.
cards.back: Social skills training helps the patients to develop interpersonal skills through role play, imitation and instruction.
cards.quote: Social skills training helps the patients to develop interpersonal skills through role play, imitation and instruction.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: ____ is given to improve the basic cognitive functions of attention, memory and executive functions.
cards.back: Cognitive retraining is given to improve the basic cognitive functions of attention, memory and executive functions.
cards.quote: Cognitive retraining is given to improve the basic cognitive functions of attention, memory and executive functions.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: After the patient improves sufficiently, ____ is given wherein the patient is helped to gain skills necessary to undertake productive employment.
cards.back: After the patient improves sufficiently, vocational training is given wherein the patient is helped to gain skills necessary to undertake productive employment.
cards.quote: After the patient improves sufficiently, vocational training is given wherein the patient is helped to gain skills necessary to undertake productive employment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: There are about ____ different types of psychotherapy.
cards.back: There are about 400 different types of psychotherapy.
cards.quote: There are about 400 different types of psychotherapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the important systems of psychotherapy.
cards.back:
Psychoanalysis
behavioural
cognitive
humanistic-existential
cards.quote: Psychoanalysis, behavioural, cognitive and humanistic-existential are the important systems of psychotherapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define therapeutic alliance.
cards.back: Therapeutic alliance is the relation between the therapist and the client in which the client has trust in the therapist and the therapist has empathy for the client.
cards.quote: Therapeutic alliance is the relation between the therapist and the client in which the client has trust in the therapist and the therapist has empathy for the client.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The predominant mode of psychotherapy for adults with psychological distress is ____ psychotherapy.
cards.back: The predominant mode of psychotherapy for adults with psychological distress is individual psychotherapy.
cards.quote: The predominant mode of psychotherapy for adults with psychological distress is individual psychotherapy.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define individual differences.
cards.back: For psychologists, individual differences refer to distinctiveness and variations among people's characteristics and behaviour patterns.
cards.quote: For psychologists, individual differences refer to distinctiveness and variations among people's characteristics and behaviour patterns.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is situationism?
cards.back: This latter view is known as situationism, which states that situations and circumstances in which one is placed influence one's behaviour.
cards.quote: This latter view is known as situationism, which states that situations and circumstances in which one is placed influence one's behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define assessment of psychological attributes.
cards.back: Assessment refers to the measurement of psychological attributes of individuals and their evaluation, often using multiple methods in terms of certain standards of comparison.
cards.quote: Assessment refers to the measurement of psychological attributes of individuals and their evaluation, often using multiple methods in terms of certain standards of comparison.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Formal vs informal assessment: the difference.
cards.back: Formal assessment is objective, standardised, and organised. On the other hand, informal assessment varies from case to case and from one assessor to another and, therefore, is open to subjective interpretations.
cards.quote: Formal assessment is objective, standardised, and organised. On the other hand, informal assessment varies from case to case and from one assessor to another and, therefore, is open to subjective interpretations.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define intelligence as a psychological attribute.
cards.back: Intelligence is the global capacity to understand the world, think rationally, and use available resources effectively when faced with challenges.
cards.quote: Intelligence is the global capacity to understand the world, think rationally, and use available resources effectively when faced with challenges.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define aptitude as a psychological attribute.
cards.back: Aptitude refers to an individual's underlying potential for acquiring skills.
cards.quote: Aptitude refers to an individual's underlying potential for acquiring skills.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define interest.
cards.back: Interest is an individual's preference for engaging in one or more specific activities relative to others.
cards.quote: Interest is an individual's preference for engaging in one or more specific activities relative to others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define personality as a psychological attribute.
cards.back: Personality refers to relatively enduring characteristics of a person that make her or him distinct from others.
cards.quote: Personality refers to relatively enduring characteristics of a person that make her or him distinct from others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define values.
cards.back: Values are enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.
cards.quote: Values are enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is a psychological test?
cards.back: Psychological Test is an objective and standardised measure of an individual's mental and/or behavioural characteristics.
cards.quote: Psychological Test is an objective and standardised measure of an individual's mental and/or behavioural characteristics.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define case study.
cards.back: Case Study is an in-depth study of the individual in terms of her/his psychological attributes, psychological history in the context of her/his psychosocial and physical environment.
cards.quote: Case Study is an in-depth study of the individual in terms of her/his psychological attributes, psychological history in the context of her/his psychosocial and physical environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is observation as an assessment method?
cards.back: Observation involves employing systematic, organised, and objective procedures to record behavioural phenomena occurring naturally in real time.
cards.quote: Observation involves employing systematic, organised, and objective procedures to record behavioural phenomena occurring naturally in real time.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the self-report method?
cards.back: Self-Report is a method in which a person provides factual information about herself/himself and/or opinions, beliefs, etc. that s/he holds.
cards.quote: Self-Report is a method in which a person provides factual information about herself/himself and/or opinions, beliefs, etc. that s/he holds.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define intelligence (Alfred Binet).
cards.back: Alfred Binet was one of the first psychologists who worked on intelligence. He defined intelligence as the ability to judge well, understand well, and reason well.
cards.quote: Alfred Binet was one of the first psychologists who worked on intelligence. He defined intelligence as the ability to judge well, understand well, and reason well.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define intelligence (Wechsler).
cards.back: Wechsler, whose intelligence tests are most widely used, understood intelligence in terms of its functionality, i.e. its value for adaptation to environment. He defined it as the global and aggregate capacity of an individual to think rationally, act purposefully, and to deal effectively with her/his environment.
cards.quote: Wechsler, whose intelligence tests are most widely used, understood intelligence in terms of its functionality, i.e. its value for adaptation to environment. He defined it as the global and aggregate capacity of an individual to think rationally, act purposefully, and to deal effectively with her/his environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Two broad approaches into which theories of intelligence are classified.
cards.back:
psychometric/structural approach
information-processing approach
cards.quote: Theories can be broadly classified as either representing a psychometric/structural approach or an information-processing approach.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychometric vs information-processing approach: the difference.
cards.back: The psychometric approach considers intelligence as an aggregate of abilities. It expresses the individual's performance in terms of a single index of cognitive abilities. On the other hand, the information-processing approach describes the processes people use in intellectual reasoning and problem solving.
cards.quote: The psychometric approach considers intelligence as an aggregate of abilities. It expresses the individual's performance in terms of a single index of cognitive abilities. On the other hand, the information-processing approach describes the processes people use in intellectual reasoning and problem solving.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which theory of intelligence did Binet propose?
cards.back: His theory of intelligence is called Uni or one factor theory of intelligence.
cards.quote: His theory of intelligence is called Uni or one factor theory of intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What did Charles Spearman propose in 1927?
cards.back: In 1927, Charles Spearman proposed a two-factor theory of intelligence employing a statistical method called factor analysis. He showed that intelligence consisted of a general factor (g-factor) and some specific factors (s-factors).
cards.quote: In 1927, Charles Spearman proposed a two-factor theory of intelligence employing a statistical method called factor analysis. He showed that intelligence consisted of a general factor (g-factor) and some specific factors (s-factors).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The ____ includes mental operations which are primary and common to all performances.
cards.back: The g-factor includes mental operations which are primary and common to all performances.
cards.quote: The g-factor includes mental operations which are primary and common to all performances.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What did Spearman call the many specific abilities in addition to the g-factor?
cards.back: In addition to the g-factor, he said that there are also many specific abilities. These are contained in what he called the s-factor.
cards.quote: In addition to the g-factor, he said that there are also many specific abilities. These are contained in what he called the s-factor.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which theory did Louis Thurstone propose, and how many abilities does it state?
cards.back: Spearman's theory was followed by Louis Thurstone's theory. He proposed the theory of primary mental abilities. It states that intelligence consists of seven primary abilities, each of which is relatively independent of the others.
cards.quote: Spearman's theory was followed by Louis Thurstone's theory. He proposed the theory of primary mental abilities. It states that intelligence consists of seven primary abilities, each of which is relatively independent of the others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name Thurstone's seven primary mental abilities.
cards.back:
Verbal Comprehension (grasping meaning of words, concepts, and ideas)
Numerical Abilities (speed and accuracy in numerical and computational skills)
Spatial Relations (visualising patterns and forms)
Perceptual Speed (speed in perceiving details)
Word Fluency (using words fluently and flexibly)
Memory (accuracy in recalling information)
Inductive Reasoning (deriving general rules from presented facts)
cards.quote: These primary abilities are: (i) Verbal Comprehension (grasping meaning of words, concepts, and ideas), (ii) Numerical Abilities (speed and accuracy in numerical and computational skills), (iii) Spatial Relations (visualising patterns and forms), (iv) Perceptual Speed (speed in perceiving details), (v) Word Fluency (using words fluently and flexibly), (vi) Memory (accuracy in recalling information), and (vii) Inductive Reasoning (deriving general rules from presented facts).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which model did Arthur Jensen propose?
cards.back: Arthur Jensen proposed a hierarchical model of intelligence consisting of abilities operating at two levels, called Level I and Level II.
cards.quote: Arthur Jensen proposed a hierarchical model of intelligence consisting of abilities operating at two levels, called Level I and Level II.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Jensen: Level I vs Level II.
cards.back: Level I is the associative learning in which output is more or less similar to the input (e.g., rote learning and memory). Level II, called cognitive competence, involves higher-order skills as they transform the input to produce an effective output.
cards.quote: Level I is the associative learning in which output is more or less similar to the input (e.g., rote learning and memory). Level II, called cognitive competence, involves higher-order skills as they transform the input to produce an effective output.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which model did J.P. Guilford propose, and along which three dimensions?
cards.back: J.P. Guilford proposed the structure-of-intellect model which classifies intellectual traits among three dimensions: operations, contents, and products.
cards.quote: J.P. Guilford proposed the structure-of-intellect model which classifies intellectual traits among three dimensions: operations, contents, and products.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the operations in Guilford's structure-of-intellect model.
cards.back:
cognition
memory recording
memory retention
divergent production
convergent production
evaluation
cards.quote: Operations are what the respondent does. These include cognition, memory recording, memory retention, divergent production, convergent production, and evaluation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the contents in Guilford's structure-of-intellect model.
cards.back:
visual
auditory
symbolic (e.g., letters, numbers)
semantic (e.g., words)
behavioural (e.g., information about people's behaviour, attitudes, needs, etc.)
cards.quote: Contents refer to the nature of materials or information on which intellectual operations are performed. These include visual, auditory, symbolic (e.g., letters, numbers), semantic (e.g., words) and behavioural (e.g., information about people's behaviour, attitudes, needs, etc.).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Name the products in Guilford's structure-of-intellect model.
cards.back:
units
classes
relations
systems
transformations
implications
cards.quote: Products refer to the form in which information is processed by the respondent. Products are classified into units, classes, relations, systems, transformations, and implications.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Since this classification (Guilford, 1988) includes 6×5×6 categories, therefore, the model has ____ cells.
cards.back: Since this classification (Guilford, 1988) includes 6×5×6 categories, therefore, the model has 180 cells.
cards.quote: Since this classification (Guilford, 1988) includes 6×5×6 categories, therefore, the model has 180 cells.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which theory did Howard Gardner propose, and what does it say intelligence is?
cards.back: Howard Gardner proposed the theory of multiple intelligences. According to him, intelligence is not a single entity; rather distinct types of intelligences exist. Each of these intelligences are independent of each other.
cards.quote: Howard Gardner proposed the theory of multiple intelligences. According to him, intelligence is not a single entity; rather distinct types of intelligences exist. Each of these intelligences are independent of each other.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is linguistic intelligence?
cards.back: It is the capacity to use language fluently and flexibly to express one's thinking and understand others.
cards.quote: It is the capacity to use language fluently and flexibly to express one's thinking and understand others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Poets and writers are very strong in which of Gardner's intelligences?
cards.back:
Linguistic
Poets and writers are very strong in this component of intelligence.
cards.quote: Poets and writers are very strong in this component of intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is logical-mathematical intelligence?
cards.back: Persons high on this type of intelligence can think logically and critically. They engage in abstract reasoning, and can manipulate symbols to solve mathematical problems.
cards.quote: Persons high on this type of intelligence can think logically and critically. They engage in abstract reasoning, and can manipulate symbols to solve mathematical problems.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is spatial intelligence?
cards.back: It refers to the abilities involved in forming, using, and transforming mental images.
cards.quote: It refers to the abilities involved in forming, using, and transforming mental images.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Pilots, sailors, sculptors, painters, architects, interior decorators and surgeons: which intelligence?
cards.back:
Spatial
Pilots, sailors, sculptors, painters, architects, interior decorators, and surgeons are likely to have highly developed spatial intelligence.
cards.quote: Pilots, sailors, sculptors, painters, architects, interior decorators, and surgeons are likely to have highly developed spatial intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is musical intelligence?
cards.back: It is the capacity to produce, create and manipulate musical patterns.
cards.quote: It is the capacity to produce, create and manipulate musical patterns.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence?
cards.back: This consists of the use of the whole body or portions of it for display or construction of products and problem solving.
cards.quote: This consists of the use of the whole body or portions of it for display or construction of products and problem solving.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Athletes, dancers, actors, sportspersons, gymnasts and surgeons: which of Gardner's intelligences?
cards.back:
Bodily-Kinaesthetic
Athletes, dancers, actors, sportspersons, gymnasts, and surgeons are likely to have such kind of intelligence.
cards.quote: Athletes, dancers, actors, sportspersons, gymnasts, and surgeons are likely to have such kind of intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is interpersonal intelligence?
cards.back: This is the ability to understand the motives, feelings and behaviours of other people so as to bond into a comfortable relationship with others.
cards.quote: This is the ability to understand the motives, feelings and behaviours of other people so as to bond into a comfortable relationship with others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Psychologists, counsellors, politicians, social workers and religious leaders: which intelligence?
cards.back:
Interpersonal
Psychologists, counsellors, politicians, social workers, and religious leaders are likely to possess high interpersonal intelligence.
cards.quote: Psychologists, counsellors, politicians, social workers, and religious leaders are likely to possess high interpersonal intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is intrapersonal intelligence?
cards.back: This refers to the knowledge of one's internal strengths and limitations and using that knowledge to effectively relate to others.
cards.quote: This refers to the knowledge of one's internal strengths and limitations and using that knowledge to effectively relate to others.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Philosophers and spiritual leaders exemplify which of Gardner's intelligences?
cards.back:
Intrapersonal
Philosophers and spiritual leaders present examples of this type of intelligence.
cards.quote: Philosophers and spiritual leaders present examples of this type of intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Gardner: what is naturalistic intelligence?
cards.back: This involves complete awareness of our relationship with the natural world.
cards.quote: This involves complete awareness of our relationship with the natural world.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Hunters, farmers, tourists, botanists, zoologists and bird watchers: which intelligence?
cards.back:
Naturalistic
Hunters, farmers, tourists, botanists, zoologists, and bird watchers possess more of naturalistic intelligence.
cards.quote: Hunters, farmers, tourists, botanists, zoologists, and bird watchers possess more of naturalistic intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define intelligence (Robert Sternberg, triarchic theory, 1985).
cards.back: Robert Sternberg (1985) proposed the triarchic theory of intelligence. Sternberg views intelligence as "the ability to adapt, to shape and select environment to accomplish one's goals and those of one's society and culture".
cards.quote: Robert Sternberg (1985) proposed the triarchic theory of intelligence. Sternberg views intelligence as "the ability to adapt, to shape and select environment to accomplish one's goals and those of one's society and culture".

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Three basic types of intelligence in the triarchic theory.
cards.back:
Componential
Experiential
Contextual
cards.quote: According to this theory, there are three basic types of intelligence: Componential, Experiential, and Contextual.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is componential (analytical) intelligence?
cards.back: Componential or analytical intelligence is the analysis of information to solve problems. Persons high on this ability think analytically and critically and succeed in schools.
cards.quote: Componential or analytical intelligence is the analysis of information to solve problems. Persons high on this ability think analytically and critically and succeed in schools.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is experiential (creative) intelligence?
cards.back: Experiential or creative intelligence is involved in using past experiences creatively to solve novel problems. It is reflected in creative performance.
cards.quote: Experiential or creative intelligence is involved in using past experiences creatively to solve novel problems. It is reflected in creative performance.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is contextual (practical) intelligence?
cards.back: Contextual or practical intelligence involves the ability to deal with environmental demands encountered on a daily basis. It may be called "street smartness" or "business sense".
cards.quote: Contextual or practical intelligence involves the ability to deal with environmental demands encountered on a daily basis. It may be called "street smartness" or "business sense".

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who developed the PASS model, and what does intellectual activity involve in it?
cards.back: This model has been developed by J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri, and Kirby (1994). According to this model, intellectual activity involves the interdependent functioning of three neurological systems, called the functional units of brain.
cards.quote: This model has been developed by J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri, and Kirby (1994). According to this model, intellectual activity involves the interdependent functioning of three neurological systems, called the functional units of brain.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is simultaneous processing?
cards.back: Simultaneous processing takes place when you perceive the relations among various concepts and integrate them into a meaningful pattern for comprehension.
cards.quote: Simultaneous processing takes place when you perceive the relations among various concepts and integrate them into a meaningful pattern for comprehension.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: In Raven's Progressive Matrices, which kind of processing helps you grasp relationships between abstract figures?
cards.back:
Simultaneous processing
For example, in Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) Test, a design is presented from which a part has been removed. You are required to choose one of the six options that best completes the design. Simultaneous processing helps you in grasping the meaning and relationship between the given abstract figures.
cards.quote: For example, in Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) Test, a design is presented from which a part has been removed. You are required to choose one of the six options that best completes the design. Simultaneous processing helps you in grasping the meaning and relationship between the given abstract figures.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is successive processing?
cards.back: Successive processing takes place when you remember all the information serially so that the recall of one leads to the recall of another.
cards.quote: Successive processing takes place when you remember all the information serially so that the recall of one leads to the recall of another.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Learning of digits, alphabets and multiplication tables are examples of which processing?
cards.back:
Successive processing
Learning of digits, alphabets, multiplication tables, etc. are examples of successive processing.
cards.quote: Learning of digits, alphabets, multiplication tables, etc. are examples of successive processing.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is planning in the PASS model?
cards.back: Planning : This is an essential feature of intelligence. After the information is attended to and processed, planning is activated. It allows us to think of the possible courses of action, implement them to reach a target, and evaluate their effectiveness.
cards.quote: Planning : This is an essential feature of intelligence. After the information is attended to and processed, planning is activated. It allows us to think of the possible courses of action, implement them to reach a target, and evaluate their effectiveness.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Which battery of tests did Das and Naglieri develop?
cards.back: Das and Naglieri have also developed a battery of tests, known as the Cognitive Assessment System (CAS).
cards.quote: Das and Naglieri have also developed a battery of tests, known as the Cognitive Assessment System (CAS).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Whose intelligence is the intelligence of adopted children more similar to?
cards.back: Another line of evidence comes from the studies of adopted children, which show that children's intelligence is more similar to their biological rather than adoptive parents.
cards.quote: Another line of evidence comes from the studies of adopted children, which show that children's intelligence is more similar to their biological rather than adoptive parents.

source.section: Intelligence: Interplay of Nature and Nurture

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What lowers intelligence, and what increases it, according to NCERT?
cards.back: There is evidence that environmental deprivation lowers intelligence while rich nutrition, good family background, and quality schooling increases intelligence.
cards.quote: There is evidence that environmental deprivation lowers intelligence while rich nutrition, good family background, and quality schooling increases intelligence.

source.section: Intelligence: Interplay of Nature and Nurture

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: There is a general consensus among psychologists that intelligence is a product of complex interaction of heredity (____) and environment (nurture).
cards.back: There is a general consensus among psychologists that intelligence is a product of complex interaction of heredity (nature) and environment (nurture).
cards.quote: There is a general consensus among psychologists that intelligence is a product of complex interaction of heredity (nature) and environment (nurture).

source.section: Intelligence: Interplay of Nature and Nurture

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who made the first successful attempt to formally measure intelligence, and when?
cards.back: In 1905, Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon, made the first successful attempt to formally measure intelligence.
cards.quote: In 1905, Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon, made the first successful attempt to formally measure intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define mental age (MA).
cards.back: In 1908, when the scale was revised, they gave the concept of Mental Age (MA), which is a measure of a person's intellectual development relative to people of her/his age group.
cards.quote: In 1908, when the scale was revised, they gave the concept of Mental Age (MA), which is a measure of a person's intellectual development relative to people of her/his age group.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define chronological age (CA).
cards.back: Chronological Age (CA) is the biological age from birth.
cards.quote: Chronological Age (CA) is the biological age from birth.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How did Binet and Simon define retardation?
cards.back: Retardation was defined by Binet and Simon as being two mental age years below the chronological age.
cards.quote: Retardation was defined by Binet and Simon as being two mental age years below the chronological age.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define IQ (William Stern, 1912).
cards.back: In 1912, William Stern, a German psychologist, devised the concept of Intelligence Quotient (IQ). IQ refers to mental age divided by chronological age, and multiplied by 100.
cards.quote: In 1912, William Stern, a German psychologist, devised the concept of Intelligence Quotient (IQ). IQ refers to mental age divided by chronological age, and multiplied by 100.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: When the MA equals the CA, the IQ equals ____.
cards.back: When the MA equals the CA, the IQ equals 100.
cards.quote: When the MA equals the CA, the IQ equals 100.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: The average IQ in the population is ____, irrespective of age.
cards.back: The average IQ in the population is 100, irrespective of age.
cards.quote: The average IQ in the population is 100, irrespective of age.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is the normal curve, and around which value is the distribution symmetrical?
cards.back: The frequency distribution for the IQ scores tends to approximate a bell-shaped curve, called the normal curve. This type of distribution is symmetrical around the central value, called the mean.
cards.quote: The frequency distribution for the IQ scores tends to approximate a bell-shaped curve, called the normal curve. This type of distribution is symmetrical around the central value, called the mean.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: People with IQ scores in the range of ____ have normal intelligence.
cards.back: People with IQ scores in the range of 90–110 have normal intelligence.
cards.quote: People with IQ scores in the range of 90–110 have normal intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: About 2 per cent have IQ above 130 and a similar share below 70. What are the two groups called?
cards.back: The persons in the first group are called intellectually gifted; those in the second group are termed intellectually disabled.
cards.quote: The persons in the first group are called intellectually gifted; those in the second group are termed intellectually disabled.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define intellectual disability (American Association on Mental Deficiency).
cards.back: The American Association on Mental Deficiency (AAMD) views intellectual disability as "significantly sub-average general intellectual functioning existing concurrently with deficits in adaptive behaviour and manifested during the developmental period".
cards.quote: The American Association on Mental Deficiency (AAMD) views intellectual disability as "significantly sub-average general intellectual functioning existing concurrently with deficits in adaptive behaviour and manifested during the developmental period".

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Define adaptive behaviour.
cards.back: Adaptive behaviour refers to a person's capacity to be independent and deal effectively with one's environment.
cards.quote: Adaptive behaviour refers to a person's capacity to be independent and deal effectively with one's environment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Levels of intellectual disability, with IQ ranges.
cards.back:
mild (IQs 55 to approximately 70)
moderate (IQs 35–40 to approximately 50–55)
severe (IQs 20–25 to approximately 35–40)
profound (IQs below 20–25)
cards.quote: The different levels of intellectual disability are: mild (IQs 55 to approximately 70), moderate (IQs 35–40 to approximately 50–55), severe (IQs 20–25 to approximately 35–40), and profound (IQs below 20–25).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What can people with moderate disability be trained in?
cards.back: The people with moderate disability lag behind their peers in language and motor skills. They can be trained in self-care skills, and simple social and communication skills.
cards.quote: The people with moderate disability lag behind their peers in language and motor skills. They can be trained in self-care skills, and simple social and communication skills.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Who began the study of gifted individuals in 1925, and with how many children?
cards.back: The study of gifted individuals began in 1925, when Lewis Terman followed the lives of about 1500 children with IQs of 130 and above to examine how intelligence was related to occupational success and life adjustment.
cards.quote: The study of gifted individuals began in 1925, when Lewis Terman followed the lives of about 1500 children with IQs of 130 and above to examine how intelligence was related to occupational success and life adjustment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Giftedness vs talent: the difference.
cards.back: Giftedness is exceptional general ability shown in superior performance in a wide variety of areas. Talent is a narrower term and refers to remarkable ability in a specific field (e.g., spiritual, social, aesthetic, etc.).
cards.quote: Giftedness is exceptional general ability shown in superior performance in a wide variety of areas. Talent is a narrower term and refers to remarkable ability in a specific field (e.g., spiritual, social, aesthetic, etc.).

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Giftedness from the teachers' point of view depends on which combination?
cards.back:
high ability
high creativity
high commitment
cards.quote: It has been suggested by psychologists that giftedness from the teachers' point of view depends on a combination of high ability, high creativity, and high commitment.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Types of intelligence tests, by basis of classification.
cards.back:
individual or group tests
verbal or performance tests
culture-fair or culture-biased
cards.quote: On the basis of their administration procedure, they can be categorised as individual or group tests. They can also be classified as either verbal or performance tests on the basis of the nature of items used. Depending upon the extent to which an intelligence test favours one culture over another, it can be judged as either culture-fair or culture-biased.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Individual vs group intelligence test: the difference.
cards.back: An individual intelligence test is one which can be administered to one person at a time. A group intelligence test can be administered to several persons simultaneously.
cards.quote: An individual intelligence test is one which can be administered to one person at a time. A group intelligence test can be administered to several persons simultaneously.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are verbal intelligence tests?
cards.back: Verbal tests require subjects to give verbal responses either orally or in a written form. Therefore, verbal tests can be administered only to literate people.
cards.quote: Verbal tests require subjects to give verbal responses either orally or in a written form. Therefore, verbal tests can be administered only to literate people.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are non-verbal intelligence tests? Name an example.
cards.back: The non-verbal tests use pictures or illustrations as test items. Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) Test is an example of a non-verbal test.
cards.quote: The non-verbal tests use pictures or illustrations as test items. Raven's Progressive Matrices (RPM) Test is an example of a non-verbal test.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What does the subject do in Raven's Progressive Matrices Test?
cards.back: In this test, the subject examines an incomplete pattern and chooses a figure from the alternatives that will complete the pattern.
cards.quote: In this test, the subject examines an incomplete pattern and chooses a figure from the alternatives that will complete the pattern.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What are performance tests?
cards.back: Performance tests require subjects to manipulate objects and other materials to perform a task. Written language is not necessary for answering the items.
cards.quote: Performance tests require subjects to manipulate objects and other materials to perform a task. Written language is not necessary for answering the items.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Kohs' Block Design Test is an example of which type of intelligence test?
cards.back:
Performance test
For example, Kohs' Block Design Test contains a number of wooden blocks. The subject is asked to arrange the blocks within a time period to produce a given design.
cards.quote: For example, Kohs' Block Design Test contains a number of wooden blocks. The subject is asked to arrange the blocks within a time period to produce a given design.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: A major advantage of performance tests is that they can be easily administered to persons from ____.
cards.back: A major advantage of performance tests is that they can be easily administered to persons from different cultures.
cards.quote: A major advantage of performance tests is that they can be easily administered to persons from different cultures.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Tests developed in America and Europe represent what cultural ethos?
cards.back: Tests developed in America and Europe represent an urban and middle class cultural ethos. Hence, educated middle class white subjects generally perform well on those tests.
cards.quote: Tests developed in America and Europe represent an urban and middle class cultural ethos. Hence, educated middle class white subjects generally perform well on those tests.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is a culture-fair test?
cards.back: It is nearly impossible to design a test that can be applied equally meaningfully in all cultures. Psychologists have tried to develop tests that are culture-fair or culturally appropriate, i.e. one that does not discriminate against individuals belonging to different cultures.
cards.quote: It is nearly impossible to design a test that can be applied equally meaningfully in all cultures. Psychologists have tried to develop tests that are culture-fair or culturally appropriate, i.e. one that does not discriminate against individuals belonging to different cultures.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What did Vygotsky argue about culture?
cards.back: Vygotsky, a Russian psychologist, has argued that culture provides a social context in which people live, grow, and understand the world around them.
cards.quote: Vygotsky, a Russian psychologist, has argued that culture provides a social context in which people live, grow, and understand the world around them.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: How do less technologically developed and technologically advanced societies differ in what they value as intelligence?
cards.back:
Social and emotional skills vs personal achievement
For example, in less technologically developed societies, social and emotional skills in relating to people are valued, while in technologically advanced societies, personal achievement founded on abilities of reasoning and judgment is considered to represent intelligence.
cards.quote: For example, in less technologically developed societies, social and emotional skills in relating to people are valued, while in technologically advanced societies, personal achievement founded on abilities of reasoning and judgment is considered to represent intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Sternberg's notion of contextual or practical intelligence implies that intelligence is a product of ____.
cards.back: Sternberg's notion of contextual or practical intelligence implies that intelligence is a product of culture.
cards.quote: Sternberg's notion of contextual or practical intelligence implies that intelligence is a product of culture.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Vygotsky: which mental functions are universal, and which are largely culture-produced?
cards.back: According to him, while elementary mental functions (e.g., crying, attending to mother's voice, sensitivity to smells, walking, and running) are universal, the manner in which higher mental functions such as problem solving and thinking operate are largely culture-produced.
cards.quote: According to him, while elementary mental functions (e.g., crying, attending to mother's voice, sensitivity to smells, walking, and running) are universal, the manner in which higher mental functions such as problem solving and thinking operate are largely culture-produced.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is technological intelligence?
cards.back: Technologically advanced societies adopt child rearing practices that foster skills of generalisation and abstraction, speed, minimal moves, and mental manipulation among children. These societies promote a type of behaviour, which can be called technological intelligence.
cards.quote: Technologically advanced societies adopt child rearing practices that foster skills of generalisation and abstraction, speed, minimal moves, and mental manipulation among children. These societies promote a type of behaviour, which can be called technological intelligence.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: Some non-western societies value self-reflection and ____ as opposed to personal achievement and individualistic orientation.
cards.back: Some non-western societies value self-reflection and collectivistic orientation as opposed to personal achievement and individualistic orientation.
cards.quote: Some non-western societies value self-reflection and collectivistic orientation as opposed to personal achievement and individualistic orientation.

cards.subject: psychology
cards.front: What is integral intelligence?
